title: Transport minister forced to take back seat at his own press conference
text:
"Do you want to ask me?"

That was the intervention from the South Australian Treasurer, just four minutes after journalists began questioning the under-fire Transport Minister Joe Szakacs over a mounting controversy.

Mr Szakacs had not faced the press pack in more than a week, amid a series of damaging revelations over the state's biggest and most expensive road infrastructure project — the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington build.

The rather convoluted "who knew what when and how could this have ever been allowed to happen" saga centres on an alleged attempt from an outlaw gang member to muscle in on a labour hire company that had won a contract on the project.

Joe Szakacs fronted the media yesterday for the first time in more than a week. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

By Tuesday afternoon, the story had made headlines for longer than than a fortnight (much to the chagrin of the tight-shipped Malinauskas Government), yet it showed no signs of slowing down, thanks to news breaking overnight that the labour hire company's contract had been terminated.

It is pertinent to note the somewhat awkward interaction between Mr Szakacs and Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis at the press conference was not spurred by reporters.

On the contrary, it appeared to be a veiled intervention on Mr Koutsantonis's behalf.

In the lead-up to it, Mr Szakacs was asked by an ABC journalist what prompted the termination of the contract.

The minister replied saying the labour hire firm had been "directed off site" for failing to advise the Torrens to Darlington Alliance of civil litigation "where one alleged shareholder was suing another alleged party who was a known bikie".

"I just want to be clear on this though, because I think …" the ABC journalist started to say, before Mr Koutsantonis quickly interjected from behind, before making his way to the microphones.

From the outset, Mr Szakacs, as both transport and infrastructure minister, was the most qualified person in the room to respond to the journalist's line of questioning.

Yet the fact his veteran colleague — the so-called "Labor Lion" and former infrastructure and transport minister — felt it necessary to take over the prickly task is a telling sign of the trouble the Malinauskas Government currently finds itself in.

Tom Koutsantonis says Joe Szakacs is an "exceptional minister with a bright future" in Tuesday's media conference. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Scandal is not a word to which the Malinauskas-led Labor team is accustomed.

In fact, not since the lead-up to the March election, when the party found itself having to defend a questionable decision to release a patient's private email to "background journalists", has it copped such sustained political heat.

Day after day of negative headlines and mounting pressure on a key minister is foreign territory for a government which has spent the past four-and-a-half years with an iron-like grip on South Australian politics.

Mr Szakacs is by no means a "junior" minister (he held various ministerial portfolios throughout the previous term), but being handed the weighty responsibility of overseeing transport and infrastructure at such a critical juncture in the Torrens to Darlington build was always going to be a step up.

Whether it is a step he has been able to make is now an open question — with the premier and his senior lieutenants being grilled on multiple occasions in the past fortnight about whether it's time for Mr Szakacs to fall on his sword, over a scandal that is not going away.

That question was one Mr Szakacs faced when he eventually made his way back to the journalists' microphones at Tuesday's press conference, where he was pressed on whether his role was tenable.

The Malinauskas government has been grilled multiple times in the past fortnight over the major road upgrade project. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"My job is to continue delivering this nation-building, state-building project," he replied, as Mr Koutsantonis nodded behind him.

"My job is to deliver it on time and on budget.

"My job is to ensure there are 5,500 South Australians who are working today because of this project.

"That is my sole focus and I am extremely dedicated and will remain so".

That may be the case.

But in the party room, Mr Szakacs has a much more nuanced job — to protect the government, and in particular Premier Peter Malinauskas, from scandal.

And whether he is currently achieving that is very much up for debate.

title: Australian banks lift interest rates
text:
Australia's lenders will apply higher interest rates to variable mortgages in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decision to hike the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent on Tuesday.

RBA governor Michele Bullock announced the cash rate was lifted to tackle persistent inflation in the Australian economy.

"It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer. Their spending can't grow very quickly because their incomes aren't growing very quickly," Ms Bullock said.

Set by the RBA, the cash rate is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks.

Put simply, it is how much it costs banks to borrow from each other.

When the RBA lifts the cash rate, it becomes more expensive for lenders to borrow from one another.

Banks respond to RBA

Macquarie Bank was the first to respond, telling customers it would raise interest rates across its variable-rate home loan products by 0.25 per cent within an hour of the RBA announcement, saying customers had until November 19 before the higher rate kicked in.

The next day, the big four banks all announced they would lift interest rates on variable home loans by 0.25 per cent.

"A 0.25 per cent per annum increase to variable home loan rates will increase monthly repayments by approximately $79 on a variable home loan of $500,000 for an owner occupier loan with principal and interest repayments," ANZ said in a statement.

Westpac, NAB, ANZ and CBA will apply the new rate from November 13.

Westpac's chief executive, consumer, Carolyn McCann said the majority of its customers were ahead in mortgage repayments.

In statements, all of the banks said customers under financial strain should contact their bank as soon as possible.

Boost for savers

Those with money in the right savings accounts will enjoy earning more interest when banks lift their rates in the middle of the month.

But as the ABC has revealed, banks have been slower to pass on rate rises to savers and often require customers to meet a number of conditions before they can "unlock" the highest rates on offer.

Comparison site Canstar said if those conditions were not met, customers reverted to a base rate of around 0.10 per cent.

Not using the right account, missing monthly minimum deposits or not meeting withdrawal conditions on the account could cause the rate to plummet to the base rate.

title: ASIC fines Mona owner David Walsh's company for late financial report
text:
The owner of Hobart's landmark Museum of Old and New Art (Mona) has been fined nearly $200,000 after his company failed to lodge a financial report on time.

David Walsh is the sole director of Downward Spiral Enterprises, the parent company of Morilla Estate, which operates Mona.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said Downward Spiral was one of 22 large companies issued with infringement notices for allegedly failing to lodge their 2025 financial reports.

Hobart's Museum of Old and New Art (MONA) lodged eight years of reporting to ASIC in June. (Facebook: MONA)

"The notices were issued as part of ASIC's ongoing surveillance and enforcement work focused on financial reporting compliance," ASIC said in a statement.

In June, the ABC revealed Downward Spiral had lodged eight years of accounts with the corporate regulator, giving a first glimpse of the finances of Mona's ultimate holding company.

The accounts from 2019 to 2025 showed more than $695 million in dividend income sustained the Mona gallery and other businesses in Mr Walsh's empire, including the Moorilla Estate winery, beer maker Moo Brew, and DarkLab, operator of the Dark Mofo festival.

They showed Downward Spiral made a profit of $63.9 million in 2024–25, largely driven by a $114 million dividend from an undisclosed source, offsetting ongoing losses from Mona.

A separate story by the ABC last year revealed Mona had racked up $408 million in losses since it opened in 2011.

Despite this, Mr Walsh insisted at the time that he was "completely happy with the finances".

Mona founder David Walsh is the sole director of Downward Spiral Enterprises. (Supplied: MONA/Jesse Hunniford)

Mona has since announced plans to establish a new art museum in Bangkok.

The ABC has sought comment from Mr Walsh via Mona.

ASIC investigation rakes in $4.3m in fines

Among the other companies fined by ASIC were hospitality firm Hemmes Group, jewellery retailer Prouds Jewellers and footwear retailer Spendless Shoes.

Each infringement notice was for $198,000.

Visitors are up, but Mona remains reliant on gambling funds Newly filed accounts give a first glimpse of Mona's ultimate holding company, showing the loss-making gallery remains heavily reliant on gambling funds.

ASIC said the 22 companies had paid a combined $4.3 million in fines.

"Payment of an infringement notice does not constitute an admission of guilt or liability," ASIC said.

"ASIC's investigation remains ongoing where companies have paid an infringement notice but still have outstanding financial reporting obligations."

ASIC said it had been conducting "data-focused surveillance" of large proprietary companies since August 2025.

DarkLab, the operator of the annual Dark Mofo festival, also falls under Downward Spiral Enterprises. (Supplied: MONA/Remi Chauvin)

In that time, it had received more than $13.7 million in infringement notice payments.

It said it had also engaged with 234 companies across a range of sectors this year, including 193 that had allegedly failed to lodge financial reports for 2025.

It said 147 companies had subsequently lodged one or more outstanding reports, with the remainder in the process of doing so.

ASIC said common reasons given for non-lodgement included audit-related issues, administrative oversight and inadequate resources to prepare financial reports.

Mona has recently added a new library, the Phrontisterion, to its offerings. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

It said some companies were unaware of their lodgement obligation until ASIC contacted them.

"Timely financial reporting gives shareholders, creditors and others dealing with a company important information about its financial position and performance, helping them make informed decisions," ASIC Commissioner Kate O'Rourke said

"Our enforcement actions over the past year send a clear message: companies must meet their financial reporting obligations and should not assume that non-compliance will go undetected.

title: David Jones on brink of collapse and behind on rent to Westfield
text:
Major Australian retailer David Jones's days could be numbered, as shopping centre Westfield confirms the department store chain has not paid rent since September and is in breach of its contracts.

A decision on the future of David Jones could be made within the next 24 hours.

The ABC understands the three-person board of the 188-year-old retailer will need to meet imminently to decide whether to put David Jones into administration.

Scentre Group, the owner of Westfield, issued a stock market update, revealing its financial exposure to the embattled department store.

David Jones has a network of 43 stores in Australia and New Zealand. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

It noted the chain occupied space at 17 Westfield locations and said David Jones had paid "all rent up to 30 September 2026".

Scentre CEO Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since September and was "therefore in breach".

Lifeline rejected, says Westfield owner

Mr Rusanow today said the shopping centre group had offered a lifeline but was knocked back by the private equity owners of David Jones.

"We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them," Mr Rusanow said.

David Jones was acquired by Anchorage Capital Partners from South African group Woolworths Holdings in late 2022.

Scentre's ASX filing noted that David Jones had provided $45 million in bank guarantees for its stores across the Westfield Australia and New Zealand portfolio, of which Scentre's share was about $30 million, equivalent to eight months' gross rent.

David Jones's key lender has chipped in extra cash to the store to stock up ahead of Christmas. (ABC News)

David Jones has a network of 43 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with flagship stores in Sydney and Melbourne CBDs, with about 50 million in-store visits a year and 5 million customers, according to its owners.

MST Marquee senior research analyst Craig Woolford said the implications of a David Jones corporate collapse would be "far-reaching".

"An administration before Christmas, if that occurs, would negatively impact December quarter profitability for retailers competing against irrational discounting," Mr Woolford said.

"While never the 'right time', stakeholders will be looking to minimise the impact and maximise any potential recoveries.

"Longer-term growth opportunities emerge for better-positioned retailers."

David Jones facing 'alarming' speculation The major retailer is being forced to defend its viability amid speculation about department store closures and disgruntled suppliers.

David Jones recently failed to file its financial accounts on time with the corporate regulator, ASIC, for a second year in a row.

If the board agreed to put the retailer into voluntary administration, thousands of jobs could be made redundant.

The news of the possible retail collapse comes a day after the Reserve Bank announced the fifth interest rate hike of 2026.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock expressed some sympathy for those on the wrong side of interest rate hikes at yesterday's press conference.

"The fact that we've had this massive shock has meant that we're poorer and that's what people are feeling," she said.

The ABC has contacted David Jones CEO Erica Berchold directly for comment.

title: China Southern Airlines suspends direct Darwin to China route after one year
text:
China Southern Airlines will suspend its direct Darwin to China flights after a year of operation, making it the latest in a suite of scrapped international routes out of Darwin.

The Darwin to Guangzhou route launched in December last year and will cease at the end of its current season, with the final flight leaving Darwin on December 3.

It was the only flight operating directly between China and the NT, and the farthest-reaching route out of the Territory.

A spokesperson from the Airport Development Group (ADG), which operates Darwin International Airport, said the call was a commercial decision by China Southern.

Direct flights from Darwin to Guangzhou were only introduced in December last year. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"Although ADG is disappointed by the airline's decision, decisions regarding individual routes and service schedules are commercial decisions made by airlines," they said.

"Travellers from Darwin continue to have connectivity to China and other international destinations through established hubs including Singapore, Denpasar and Dili."

The flight is the latest in a series of short-lived international routes out of Darwin.

In 2025, Qantas launched a direct flight between Darwin and Singapore while AirAsia introduced services from Darwin to Bali and Kuala Lumpur.

By June 2026, Qantas had reduced its Darwin to Singapore flights to cover the peak tourism season only, while AirAsia had pulled out of Darwin entirely.

Darwin International Airport continues to connect passengers to Singapore, Denpasar and Dili. (Facebook: Darwin International Airport)

The ADG spokesperson said it is exploring other international flight routes out of the Territory capital.

"ADG continues to actively engage with airline carriers and other aviation partners about opportunities to strengthen Darwin's international connectivity," they said.

'We're shouting at the clouds'

Announced in August 2025, the Darwin to Guangzhou route was heralded as a boost to tourism which would deliver 52,000 seats between the two cities each year.

In April this year, Tourism Minister Marie-Clare Boothby led a delegation of tourism operators to Guangzhou for talks with travel agents.

"This mission was about showing that we are serious about growing our share of the Chinese traveller market," she said at the time.

Marie-Clare Boothby said the Darwin to China route was about growing tourism in the NT. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"China — and particularly Guangzhou and the wider Guangdong province — offers the Territory a high-value and highly concentrated market."

Northern Territory Chamber of Commerce CEO Glen Hingley, however, says the axing impacts more than just the tourism industry.

"I think all businesses across the Northern Territory and, in particular, those that were looking to evolve and grow are disappointed with this decision," he said.

Mr Hingley said stakeholders across the NT needed to collaborate, making flight routes in and out of Darwin viable for trade as well as tourism.

"It's important that for these airlines when they make decisions to come here that they're not just looking at passengers, they're looking at the freight opportunities," he said.

Glen Hingley says airline operators should be looking at freight opportunities as well as passengers. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We're the only destination that was flying a 737, the rest of Australia has wide-bodied aircraft, so they're able to make it work from a freight perspective."

Mr Hingley said there was ample opportunity for the NT aviation industry and that overcoming the challenge of its small population required cooperation across sectors.

"We've got to not operate in silos, whether that's different government agencies, different industry bodies, different industry sectors, and of course the airport," he said.

"We're shouting at clouds if we're waiting for the federal government to intervene."

title: Fake jobs and malicious code used by hackers in largest crypto-heist
text:
The world's largest crypto-exchange platform says attackers used fake job interviews and malicious code to steal $US6.6 billion ($9 billion) in funds.

The attack on Binance, believed to be the largest cyber attack in the cryptocurrency sector's history, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply.

The FBI has attributed the four-hour attack on October 29 to North Korea-affiliated hackers.

North Korea has denied the allegations, with the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un calling the claim "absurd rhetoric".

Who is behind crypto heist? Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack?

How it unfolded

Binance said the hackers began their plans as early as June.

It said they first targeted a platform engineer by getting them to download a virus-laden version of the widely known programming software Homebrew.

Binance's cybersecurity teams identified the malware and removed it, but the hackers had already had time to harvest information about the engineer and his colleagues.

Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

In September, the attackers approached another Binance engineer through a legitimate job-search platform, offering him an interview for a position in a fictitious company.

After building trust with the subject through sharing social media photos and videos, they asked the engineer to download a test exercise as part of the interview process.

The exercise contained malware that deployed "sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques", Binance said, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version.

That malware was critical to the success of the attack, as it allowed the hackers to establish a connection with Binance's internal systems.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

On October 20, the attackers used the access they had gained and an internal AI tool to gain control over software used by two other engineers.

Nine days later, they triggered malicious code that initiated the attack.

According to Binance, 98 per cent of the affected assets have been replenished by drawing on its own funds, with the remaining amount involving little-traded currencies that are harder to acquire.

It said around one-third of the stolen assets had been frozen, meaning the attackers could not use them or convert them to another currency.

AFP

title: Staggs says he means no harm by refusing to sing Australian anthem
text:
Kotoni Staggs says his decision not to sing the national anthem comes from a place of respect, as he and his Kangaroos teammates find themselves at the centre of a culture war.

Staggs and several fellow Australia team members, who will face Samoa in Sunday's World Cup semifinal at the Sydney Football Stadium, have been criticised throughout the tournament because of their refusal to sing the pre-game anthem.

The Brisbane centre received the backing of Broncos teammate Pat Carrigan for his stance, hoping the decision would open up a wider discussion about Australia's history.

Kangaroos pile on the points in World Cup thrashing of Cook Islands The Kangaroos go undefeated through the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup as they close out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.

Staggs, who has won nine caps for the Kangaroos since his debut in 2023, said: "I'm a proud Wirajudri boy and I'm proud of who I am and where I come from, and me not singing an anthem doesn't mean that I'm not grateful.

"I still love wearing that jersey. When the anthem is getting played you look around and get emotional.

"But me not singing, it's a whole different meaning to that and that's just me."

Staggs said his position on singing Advance Australia Fair came from wanting to honour his ancestors.

"Obviously in the past and what happened back in the day I've just learned from that," Staggs said.

"You also talk to your elders from back home and grandparents and stuff and [understand] what they had to go through. It's more of a respect for my elders and my family.

Kotoni Staggs says his refusal to sing the national anthem does not take away from his love of representing Australia. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"I'm a proud Australian as well but at the end of the day it's just something that I've lived by, and I've got no harm in it. It doesn't take anything away from the jersey I wear."

Criticism of Staggs and other Indigenous Kangaroos stars, including Latrell Mitchell, is nothing new.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner, a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, has also stressed the importance of walking out alongside the Australian, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island flags during the World Cup.

"All three flags have separate meanings for our country, and it represents that we're a diverse country with many different cultures," she said.

Jillaroos players hold the Torres Strait Island flag over their shoulders during a national anthem at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Our team, in particular, this 23, and our staff come from all different walks of life and cultural backgrounds, and we celebrate that diversity. That's a reflection of our country.

"You know, the blue flag is really important to everybody, just as equally as our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flag.

"So when you look at the values of that and you educate yourself about those flags, then you can't help but be passionate to be a proud Australian."

Former Australian Test coach Mal Meninga previously defended players for their firm stance on the matter of the anthem.

Carrigan is of the opinion athletes should have the right to stand up for what they believe in.

Pat Carrigan says players should have the freedom to stand up for their beliefs. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"As sports people there's a focus on us as role models, but it probably points to a greater conversation for us to have as a society outside of football," Carrigan said.

"And about the reason why the boys feel the way about the anthem and perhaps our history as a country too.

"I know that each and every boy here is proud to pull on the green and gold.

"People may say it's represented in singing an anthem. I love Australia and I'm proud to pull on this jersey and I love running out with these guys too.

"I think it's a unique opportunity in sport that we get to be role models and voice opinions on different things, and maybe that's a way for us to look at ourselves as a country and how we can continue to come together."

AAP/ABC

title: Lobster fishers rail against salmon industry's antibiotic plans
text:
Tensions have escalated between Tasmania's salmon industry and the wild seafood sector over plans to close some fishing areas when antibiotics are used in salmon pens.

Salmon Tasmania has applied for an emergency permit to use florfenicol to treat farmed fish affected by a bacterial disease that caused mass mortalities in 2025.

A separate emergency permit issued late last year had to be revoked in March after traces of florfenicol were detected in wild seafood more than 10 kilometres away.

The new permit application includes a plan to shut wild fisheries for up to six weeks if they are located within the same zone as salmon pens treated with antibiotics.

The closures are designed to avoid trade bans being imposed by countries that have zero tolerance for antibiotics in rock lobster, abalone and other wild seafood.

The Tasmanian Atlantic salmon farming industry has been hard hit by disease. (Tassal)

Under the "Wild Fisheries Market Access Plan", Salmon Tasmania would also provide financial support to affected commercial fishers to ensure they were no worse off.

But lobster fisherman Bryce Way said he and others in his sector were opposed to any reduction in their access to fisheries.

"You've got this introduced species coming around wanting to shut our areas," Mr Way told ABC Mornings.

"And it's just not fair. It just makes no sense to us how they think it is right to do."

Once implemented, Mr Way said he doubted the closures would be limited to six weeks in future years.

Loading...

"Where's it end?" he said.

"It's only four to six weeks now. What's next year, 12 weeks?"

Mr Way said he and others were willing to disrupt the salmon industry through large-scale protests.

" If the salmon industry thinks that five kayaks and one dinghy was disruptive, what do you think is going to happen when you get 150, 200 commercial boats? "

He said no amount of compensation would make up for losing access to fisheries.

"If you're accepting money, you're selling your soul," he said. "That's all you're doing.

" If you care about the industry, you shouldn't be accepting any dollar value to have an area closed. "

Bryce Way says that if the salmon industry was inconvenienced by small protests (above), it should consider what a large-scale action might cause. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

Tasmanian Rock Lobster Council president Danny Fox said Mr Way's concerns were shared by many across the sector.

"They're not too happy, the fishermen," Mr Fox told the Country Hour.

"The sentiment's pretty poor."

He said there were no plans to "block" the salmon industry, but he would not rule out protests.

" Most fishermen are happy to see the salmon industry there, and it's just got to play by the rules, and they've got to stay in their own lane a little bit more. "

Salmon pens managed by Huon Aquaculture at Surveyors Bay. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

'Very, very small part' of wild fisheries affected

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) is expected to make a decision on Salmon Tasmania's emergency use permit later this month.

Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said, if approved, florfenicol would only be used in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel and Storm Bay when recommended by veterinarians.

"When you look at the areas that would be closed if we were using florfenicol … [it's] a very, very small part of their [wild] fishery," he told ABC Mornings.

John Whittington says the salmon industry is also working on options to minimise the use of antibiotics. (ABC News: Madeleine Rojahn)

Dr Whittington said Salmon Tasmania was in discussions with all trade-exposed fishing sectors about the proposed compensation plan.

These include the lobster, abalone, oyster and periwinkle and urchin sectors.

"What we're looking to do is work with the sectors to develop an industry support program that ensures that if there is any out-of-pocket cost as a result of a closure for florfenicol, those fishers are made good through the process."

The first licence to use florfenicol in Atlantic salmon farms was revoked after traces were found in non-target species kilometres away from where it was deployed. (Abbey Laboratories)

Dr Whittington said the industry was also working on options to minimise the use of antibiotics, including a selective breeding program, vaccinations and improved feeds.

"Ideally, when those vaccines are fully efficacious, when the selective breeding program has really established itself, we will be managing this disease without the need for therapeutants."

A total of 5.4 tonnes of florfenicol was used last summer, during which about 9,000 tonnes of salmon still died.

Tasmania's health department has said there were no reports of adverse human health effects from eating seafood with florfenicol residues.

However, as a precaution, it has said people can avoid seafood caught within 3km of a treated salmon pen.

Pharmaceutical company Abbey Labs has applied to the regulator for a separate "minor use" permit to increase the dose rate and treatment regime of florfenicol.

It also wants to expand the geographical use of florfenicol to salmon pens at Oakhampton Bay, on the state's east coast.

title: Melbourne Salvos cafe closes as demand exceeds capacity
text:
A social service cafe in Melbourne's inner west has closed its doors five months after it opened, as its operator scrambles to find a new location.

The Salvation Army's Lighthouse Cafe opened in May to provide vulnerable Footscray community members with free meals and connection to homelessness, mental health, and drug and alcohol support.

The Salvation Army said the service was relocating due to high demand, which rendered the current space unsuitable.

"We've been overwhelmed by the need," The Salvation Army Melbourne Commanding Officer Major Brendan Nottle told 774 ABC Melbourne Breakfast.

"We're seeing 170 people on average a day come through that cafe, and initially we were expecting 50 to 60.

"Even in the first couple of weeks we were thinking, 'We've got a problem here', because it's one single room and it wasn't big enough to accommodate the number of people coming through."

The Salvation Army says the venue could only cater for less than half of the 170 people attending each day. (ABC News: Tim Callanan)

A man who used the service, who wanted to be known as PJ, said he and others were "pissed off and angry" the doors had shut.

"It's just wrong, man," he said.

"Everyone here is malnourished."

He said everyone loved the cafe.

" The meals were beautiful, the staff were beautiful. "

He said he was upset by the lack of follow-through for the service.

"We were promised a long-term cafe," he said.

"They don't follow-through … they just disappear."

Search for new home for Lighthouse in Footscray

The project had so far received $350,000 from the state government, with another $576,000 earmarked.

Major Nottle said while a new location had not been found, The Salvation Army was committed to keeping the service in Footscray, where the organisation has had a presence since 1887.

"We're relocating to another site that will be more suitable to the work we want to do, not just in terms of being able to accommodate more people in the cafe, but also having additional spaces where we can co-locate with other services," Major Nottle said.

Major Brendan Nottle with local MP Katie Hall at Lighthouse Cafe earlier this year. (Supplied: Project 614)

He acknowledged there had been concerns from surrounding businesses around safety.

"Have there been a couple of complaints from neighbours? Yes, there have," he said.

"But for every complaint there's been three or four really positive comments from people who are overwhelmed emotionally because of the support they were receiving."

The temporary closure comes as The Salvation Army works to wind down Foley House, a long-term residential facility that has provided beds for homeless men since 2013.

The Salvation Army has said the accommodation would close once the final resident "has been matched with safe, suitable and affordable accommodation".

"Foley House has, due to the complexity of the residents, become a disability-like accommodation without access to any form of accommodation funding other than The Salvation Army itself," the organisation said at the time.

Footscray Community Response's Shifrah Blustein said the closure of the cafe would make people's lives harder.

A Footscray resident says he is angry that the cafe has closed. (ABC News: Tim Callanan)

"Having somewhere you can go for a meal, to not be cold or feel the heat from outside is something, but, at the end of the day, these people need to be supported into housing.

"Providing a few outreach workers or a cafe, it isn't a replacement for housing.

"The community just wants some very, very basic services to be delivered to people doing it so tough on the streets who are being blamed and dehumanised for every social problem under the sun in Footscray.

"This was one tiny measure to address that, in a very sort of superficial way, I guess, to have a place where people could be off the street, be fed, and they can't even sustain that."

The Salvation Army said an interim "mobile and on foot" service would start later this month to provide food relief and connection with support services.

title: Gold Coast triple header as Tszyu goes for two-weight glory
text:
Tim Tszyu will headline a stacked triple-header boxing card at Robina Stadium on the Gold Coast.

The 32-year-old will look to become a two-weight world champion when he takes on Cuban-American fighter Erislandy Lara for the WBA middleweight world title on December 13.

That is one of three all-star fights to take place on the night though, with former undisputed super welterweight world champion Jermell Charlo (35-2-1) stepping into the ring for the first time in three years when he takes on Australian power puncher Brock Jarvis (23-1).

Liam Wilson (18-3) will also meet Elnur Samedov (22-1) for the WBA super featherweight world title.

"This is the biggest and best fight card in Australia, full stop," No Limit Boxing chief executive George Rose said.

"A reigning world champion, a former undisputed world champion and two world titles, in a stadium on the Gold Coast. Nothing else comes close."

Tszyu (28-3) has enjoyed a career resurgence since stepping up to middleweight, winning his last three fights at the weight following a run of three defeats in four at light middleweight.

The Australian was crowned WBO light middleweight champion on the Gold Coast in 2023, defeating Brian Mendoza after being elevated from interim champion in the lead up.

His last stadium fight took place in Townsville against Jeff Horn in 2020.

Tim Tszyu is the WBO International Super Middleweight Title holder. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

"This is what I live for," Tszyu said in a statement.

"Lara is a great champion and one of the most avoided fighters in the world. That is exactly why I wanted him. Spence was the first step. This is the one that matters.

"Queensland and the Gold Coast have always backed me.

"I'm ready to take that belt off Lara on the Gold Coast."

Lara (32-3-3), the 43-year-old veteran southpaw, is a two-division world champion and has been the WBA middleweight world champion since 2021.

The former amateur world champion has made four successful defences of the belt, including knocking out Michael Zerafa in two rounds in Las Vegas in 2024.

"Tim Tszyu wanted the best middleweight in the world," Rose said.

"And we got him."

Lara, like Tszyu, has three career defeats, all via the scorecards, losing by majority decision to Paul Williams and split decision defeats to Canelo Álvarez and Jarrett Hurd.

"I'm going to Australia with one goal … to defend my title, put on a great performance and give the fans a fight they'll remember for a long time," Lara said.

Charlo was supposed to fight Tszyu in 2023 before a broken hand scuppered those plans.

Jermell Charlo (right) has not fought in three years. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

The then WBA, WBC, IBF and WBO light middleweight champion had been set to fight Tszyu despite the hand injury, only for him to repeatedly delay and ultimately pull out to face Álvarez at super middleweight instead.

Charlo famously said fighting Tszyu "does nothing for my career" by way of explanation, however fighting and losing to Álvarez ultimately cost the American all four of his belts, with the 36-year-old looking to restart his career in Australia.

"I've heard all the talk, and now it's time to remind everybody why Jermell Charlo is still him," Charlo said.

"I'm willing to fight on a co-main event all the way in Australia because that's how hungry I am. I've got so much in me and I wasn't going to let this year end without giving my fans what they've been waiting for."

Jarvis, who has 21 knock out wins in his 24 fights, said his aim was to "ruin" Charlo's comeback.

In the other world title fight, Liam Wilson (18-3), who fought at the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, will meet Azerbaijani fighter Samedov.

Liam Wilson has twice challenged for the world title. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Wilson is a two-time world title challenger who came agonisingly close to winning the world title in 2023 and 2024 against Emanuel Navarrete and Oscar Valdez respectively.

"I have chased this shot around the world," Wilson said.

"My career hasn't been easy but I've felt the love from fans every step of the way. I have never backed down from anyone and I am not starting now.

"Samedov is the champion. Good. Taking it off the champion means more.

"I boxed for Australia on the Gold Coast at the Commonwealth Games almost a decade ago. Now, I get the chance to win a world title in the same city. You can't not love that."

He has spoken publicly several times since he was traded in October, a year after his initial bid failed, declaring a motivating factor to join the Hawks was team success. Veteran forward Jack Gunston said Merrett would be a versatile weapon, having been used, at times, at half-back by the Bombers this year.

“He’s a quality player. Sunny Side Sandwiches has evolved over the years. The menu has expanded, and then been reduced. Certain sangers have come, and then gone again. But according to co-owner Mack Bowers, there’s one that hasn’t changed – the eggplant sandwich. The Sunny Side eggplant sandwich Morgan Roberts Sunny Side Sandwiches Don’t know Sunny Side Sandwiches? Are you sure? Because it can sometimes feel like it’s everywhere on socials.

Advertisement

That’s perhaps because of the fairly steady clip at which it has been launching and relaunching venues – Windsor in 2021, Paddington in 2023, a slick refurb of Windsor in April this year, and East Brisbane in June. But also, the sandwiches at these neatly branded stores are very, very good. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Popular CBD French diner closes suddenly It took this column a while to wrap its head around just how good Sunny Side is. When we first tried its sandwiches in 2023 we liked, rather than loved them. Even the signature chicken schnitty sandwich needs to be ordered the right way, which is to slip some gooey American cheese between the two slices of schnitzel, which lifts it from very good to exceptional. But the sandwiches have evolved. Most importantly, Bowers and co-owner Charline De Conto (the two are married) have made their own Hokkaido-style shokupan bread. You could argue it’s key to how good these sandwiches are. The schnitty sandwich and the eggplant sandwich. Morgan Roberts

Advertisement

The star of this triple-store setup is, no doubt, the Sunny Side classic chicken schnitty sandwich, but we don’t think it’s the most impressive. Not quite. Instead, that honour belongs to the shop’s eggplant sandwich. The Sunny Side Sandwiches eggplant sandwich “The eggplant sandwich has been there since day one,” Bowers says. “It’s one of my favourite sandwiches. It has all the best bits of the classic schnitty, but for vegetarians. “It’s funny because I often say to people, ‘It’s something that you should definitely try once,’ because once we’ve prepared it, it really has as much going on as the chicken schnitty, but in this different format.” Bowers is right. A serious amount of prep goes into this sandwich. The eggplant is sliced, bathed in salt water, and panko crumbed. And then, instead of going into the fryer, it goes into the freezer.

Advertisement

Sunny Side Sandwiches in East Brisbane. Morgan Roberts “Sometimes when you put them in a fryer at room temperature, it’s quite violent for a thin little piece of eggplant and it can break up. And when you freeze them, they actually keep their shape better,” he says. Then, once out of the fryer, it’s built the same way as the chicken schnitty: two slices of eggplant with the optional American cheese slapped in the middle; chopped iceberg lettuce dressed in Japanese mayo, dill, parsley and chives; bread and butter pickles; shokupan bread; and then a “magic sprinkle” of the shop’s signature seasoning, which features salt, nutritional yeast, Korean chilli flakes and “a few other little secret herbs and spices.” Co-owner Mack Bowers. Morgan Roberts A contender for Brisbane’s best vegetarian sanger

Advertisement

Listen, it really is up there. And, like Bowers says, it’s worth trying even if you’re not vegetarian. There’s so much to like about it: the crispness of the eggplant, the crunch of the iceberg, the acid of the pickles, the velvety texture of the mayo with its tangy stack of herbs. And then there’s the deep, deep umami of the “magic sprinkle”. Still, for us, the shokupan is the real star here. It’s baked in-house, meaning it’s ultra-consistent, and able to be sliced thinly while maintaining its integrity. The eggplant sandwich was perhaps never going to outshine the schnitty – few sandwiches around town could, to be fair – but you still need to try it. And if you’re with a mate, the power move is of course to order both and split them between you. Where to get it The eggplant sandwich is $18.80. You can get one from 1007 Stanley Street East, East Brisbane; 173A Latrobe Terrace, Paddington; and Shop 203/142 Newmarket Road, Windsor.

BlackMilk Clothing, a cult favourite fashion brand created 17 years ago in Brisbane that enjoyed global success, has fallen into administration, the company revealed. At the height of its popularity, the brand’s pop culture themed collections would sell out within minutes. BlackMilk Clothing has gone into voluntary administration. Ashley Joncas Photography “This is not an announcement I ever imagined having to make, and I wanted you to hear it directly from me,” Linda Lillis said in a Facebook post on Wednesday.

“What started as a side hobby at our kitchen table became a global brand and a community that has meant so much to our family. “I’m incredibly proud of what BlackMilk has created over those 17 years. David Jones’ private equity owners are on the cusp of appointing voluntary administrators as soon as Thursday morning after talks with major landlord Scentre fell over when the department store failed to pay rent for October. Westfield owner Scentre Group, which operates 17 shopping centres in which the prestige department store is located, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors, according to a source close to negotiations but not authorised to speak publicly. A deal to save the 188-year-old retailer David Jones may be unwinding. Louise Kennerley David Jones’ board directors are now assessing how long the 188-year-old retailer can continue trading before it appoints a voluntary administrator, which is expected to be McGrathNicol, the source said. Chief executive Erica Berchtold and board directors Phillip Cave and Simon Woodhouse, who are executive chair and managing partner at private equity firm Anchorage Capital respectively, were convening a board meeting on Wednesday evening, with a decision on voluntary administration expected to be made by Thursday morning.

Advertisement

Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since October and “therefore are in breach”. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it “We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading,” Rusanow said in a statement. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them.” David Jones’ initial restructuring deal to Scentre Group initially proposed handing over nine stores from February, keeping three stores at rents of 8 per cent of sales, continuing five stores on current terms, and unlocking $45 million in bank guarantees in exchange for equity. “It’s a straight financial calculation as to how they can continue trading,” the source said. “Do they meet the solvency test? They need to sit down and discuss the finances.”

Advertisement

David Jones’ failure to pay rent for October was a key flashpoint in why talks with Scentre Group fell over, a source said. Other commercial property landlords are also owed rent. A spokesman for David Jones confirmed that talks between the group and Scentre failed to resolve the impasse and talks had now concluded. “We know what you know.” A David Jones staff member who declined to be identified. The retailer’s stores in Westfield Parramatta, Warringah Mall, Carindale in NSW, Indooroopilly Shopping Centre, Robina Town Centre, Sunshine Plaza in Queensland, Westfield Marion in South Australia, Westfield Doncaster, Southland, Carousel, Booragoon in Victoria, and Karrinyup Shopping Centre in Western Australia are suspected as earmarked for closure, according to analysis by financial services firm MST Marquee.

A sense of impending trouble has already pervaded some stores. Loss-making store Westfield Parramatta in western Sydney was exceptionally quiet when this publication visited on Wednesday morning. Few shoppers were browsing across both levels of the store. The further in, the quieter it became.

Advertisement

At the back on level one, near the birthday cards and beds, temporary cardboard panels created a wall with a sign reading “staff only beyond this point”. Through gaps in the makeshift screen, shelves, mannequins and a selection of stock including Christmas trees and suitcases could be seen, stored away from the public eye. A makeshift wall set up in David Jones’ Parramatta store. Behind it is stock, shelves and mannequins. Signs advertising Black Friday sale offers, which expire in early December, had been collected and placed onto one of the counters. It’s unclear if staff were about to put them up or had just taken them down. Store staff were reluctant to talk and declined to confirm if it would be closing, with one employee saying: “We know what you know”. On Wednesday, David Jones’ lender Hilco said in a statement: “Hilco Capital has had no formal update on the status of negotiations.”

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘Alarming’: David Jones workers brace for job losses as store closures loom Hilco Capital confirmed last week that it had provided additional funding to see it through December, traditionally the most crucial time of the year for department stores. “Hilco Capital has funded above the agreed facility to allow David Jones to increase stock holdings ahead of the busy Christmas trade and sales period,” a Hilco spokesperson said. The group had also been negotiating with multiple landlords to slash its rent bill and close some loss-making stores. Lease and rent costs totalled $125 million for the 2025 financial year, but its debt burden also weighed heavily on the group with finance costs totalling $153 million, financial accounts released earlier this year show. Suppliers have told this publication they were already restricting the financial terms of sales to David Jones due to lengthening payment terms. They will become unsecured creditors and potentially lose significantly on any outstanding bills if the retailer goes into administration.

Advertisement

ASX-listed retailer Accent Group confirmed it moved to cash-on-delivery after outstanding unpaid invoices earlier this year, which David Jones has since resolved. Menswear label M.J. Bale ceased supplying David Jones’ online store, but still operates about nine concessions on the retailer’s premises. Dozens of premium and designer labels have jumped ship to rival Myer over the past few months. If David Jones collapses, Myer’s sales could be boosted by as much as $180 million and specialty retailers like JB Hi-Fi and Rebel may benefit from rent cuts, analysis from MST Marquee suggests. David Jones is the country’s 12th-largest retailer by floor space, ahead of Chemist Warehouse. “Myer has 12 stores within close proximity to the likely closed David Jones stores. Up to half of the lost David Jones sales could switch to Myer,” MST Marquee analysts said. “If landlords aren’t able to backfill the space effectively, lower rents across specialty retailers may result.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. A shark behaviour expert says a $100,000 Gold Coast plan for night surfing by floodlights near the mouth of a river known for bull sharks might not be such a great idea. Gold Coast City Council discussed trialling the concept – where three 24-metre-high lights would illuminate the water, so surfers can keep catching waves into the night – during next year’s World Surfing event at Snapper Rocks. The trial is part of a wider “Surfing Infrastructure Masterplan” hatched to maximise profit off the coast’s famous beaches, with the council keen to see how night surfing would work in action. Griffith University shark expert Vincent Raoult said bull sharks, which are known to be around the Tweed River outflow next to Snapper Rocks, are active at night, particularly between 4pm and 10pm.

Advertisement

Raoult said a one-off event would probably be fine, but more permanent or reoccurring night surfing at Snapper Rocks would be asking for trouble. “Anyone who has done any fishing knows that if you have lights on the side of the boat into the water, you’re going to bring up a whole host of bait fish, and often with those bait fish, you’ll have sharks coming in as well,” he said. Kelly Slater surfing at night … in the safety of his wave pool. Kenny Morris/World Surf League “Those floodlights will have essentially the same effect.” He said any plans should not be compared with France, where the WSL has held night surfing before.

Advertisement

“The key difference is in France there are no sharks,” he said. Related Article Triathlon Swim leg of Noosa triathlon cancelled after multiple shark sightings The plan was discussed in a transport and infrastructure meeting at the council on Tuesday, and follows the swim leg of the popular Noosa Triathlon being called off over the weekend due to shark sightings. Speaking with Nine News on Tuesday, councillor Gail O’Neill said precautions would be taken to make sure night surfing was safe. “With all the surfing events and all the surf life-saving events we have, people are on jet skis making sure sharks aren’t in the area,” she said.

Advertisement

But Raoult said the most successful shark-spotting tactic on the Gold Coast would be unavailable after dusk. “Drones can’t really work at night – you can’t really see through the water, and there are also some flight restrictions around operating drones at night,” he said. Whether the plan goes ahead is up to the World Surfing League, with the council offering to pay for the lights. title: How Labor’s Riverton MLA has snookered himself

November 4, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jagadish Krishnan is having a bet both ways when he says he has done “everything appropriately” when declaring gifts, while simultaneously claiming he’s no longer a businessman outside parliament. An investigation by 9News and WAtoday revealed the WA Labor MP is being sued for $1 million in a US court. Riverton MLA Jagadish Krishnan. Hamish Hastie Wall Street investor Kannan Amalraj lent Krishnan the money for his wife’s businesses Spectrum Health and Codd Technology, and is now suing him, claiming he hasn’t paid it back. The American businessman also claims to have bankrolled Krishnan’s lavish trip to New York City in May 2024, covering thousands of dollars worth of expenses.

Advertisement

Accommodation, including a luxury $1000-a-night hotel metres from Times Square, limousine and taxi services, and a dinner cruise on the Hudson River. This masthead has seen receipts that back up some of these claims. The rest are detailed in a writ filed in the New Jersey District Court. All up, it totals approximately $6000 worth of alleged gifts. Nickels and dimes compared to the size of the loan, but what is in question is whether Krishnan should have declared it on the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. In a bizarre and hastily organised press conference last week, Krishnan defended himself, declaring he had “done everything appropriately in my declarations”. Under the Members of Parliament Act 1992, a member “shall disclose gifts received”, if they are valued at $500 or more. This includes travel undertaken by the member unless it “was made in the ordinary course of any trade, profession or vocation of the Member”.

Advertisement

He is claiming the travel gifts were for business purposes and exempt from declaration. But he has publicly declared he ceded his business roles when he entered parliament in 2021. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament Labor’s Riverton MP spends nearly entire salary on electorate expenses “Once I entered politics, I resigned from being a director,” Krishnan told 9News just last year, days out from the state election. “I have been out of business for almost four years.” He remains a shareholder of various interests, but the Australian Tax Office does not deem a shareholder to be a trade, profession or vocation.

Advertisement

Either, Krishnan is actually still involved in his businesses, which would absolve him of his responsibility to declare financial contributions. Or, he really is no longer a businessman, in which case he must declare the gifts. The Labor MP has snookered himself. Geoffrey Watson SC, director of Centre for Public Integrity, said MPs should regard their parliamentary role as their full-time employment. “They’re effectively an employee of the people of Western Australia,” he told WAtoday.

Advertisement

Or, in other words, a court case on the other side of the world does not absolve Krishnan of his responsibility and obligation to be accountable and transparent to his constituents. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament The US trip at the heart of WA Labor MP’s court fight over $1 million loan Krishnan has not responded to detailed questions about his financial dealings. Some are, understandably, covered by the fact that there are legal proceedings under way. But other unanswered questions are not, including is he bankrupt? (Which would render a member ineligible to sit in parliament). Let’s not forget that Krishnan was parliamentary secretary to the premier at the time of the trip – Roger Cook’s right-hand man – when he lobbied overseas investors for a big loan by any measure for his wife’s company, enjoying lavish gifts from an investor looking to sink his claws into the Australian market.

Advertisement

This masthead does not suggest he was on official parliamentary businesses while in the US, or that taxpayers footed any travel bill. Cook’s response when asked if Krishnan – and all members of his party – would face punishment if he hadn’t upheld the necessary standards of disclosures was unimpressively unconvincing. “That’s a hypothetical … that’s a decision for the caucus,” Cook said. The premier, like his colleagues, is watching this play out, because they aren’t sure which side of the court battle is telling the truth. For now, the US Federal Court will decide that.

Advertisement

But it does not say much if Cook cannot even tell his caucus to uphold basic parliamentary standards or face some sort of discipline. Let alone a parliamentary inquiry into Krishnan’s conduct.

Four years after Samoa was crushed in the World Cup final by Australia, captain Junior Paulo says he is desperate to avenge the loss and pull off the nation’s greatest win against the Kangaroos at Allianz Stadium on Sunday. “To lose a grand final like that … I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t burning for the guys who were there,” Paulo said of that 30-10 defeat at Old Trafford in 2022. The Kangaroos beat Samoa in the 2022 Rugby League World Cup final in England. Getty There’s been a few changes to the Samoan team in that time. Josh Papali’i has retired and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has gone from playing fullback to switching codes and joining the Wallabies. But the bulk of Samoa’s backline remains, including five-eighth and co-captain Jarome Luai, winger Brian To’o and centre Stephen Crichton. As does Spencer Leniu, who will again be injected off the bench to provide some spark and power.

Paulo, the 32-year-old 123kg wrecking-ball, said victory over Kevin Walters’ Kangaroos would rank among the country’s greatest feats. “It’s a privilege to be in this position for us,” he said. “It’s an opportunity to be a part of history and hopefully what can be one of the biggest upsets.” Junior Paulo says he has a “burning” desire to avenge the 2022 World Cup final defeat. Getty Images Paulo said fatigued would not be an issue, despite Samoa’s gruelling 20-18 defeat to Tonga being played 24 hours after the Kangaroos proved far too good for Karmichael Hunt’s Cook Islands. “We’ve had a good couple of days just to emotionally regulate [after the] immense pressure that came with the game as well,” Paulo said.

One area where Samoa will likely attack the Kangaroos is through the middle. New Zealand smashed Australia up front in their narrow 24-22 loss in the tournament opener, while Fiji and the Cook Islands also physically put Walters’ side under huge pressure. Former Kangaroos playmaker Luke Keary described Australia’s struggles in the middle as “concerning”. But Paulo downplayed the Kangaroos’ Achilles heel. “There’s still a quality forward pack right across the park,” he said.

Meanwhile, Australia centre Kotoni Staggs claims his decision not to sing the national anthem comes from a place of respect. Staggs and several fellow Australia team members have been criticised throughout the tournament because of their refusal to sing the pre-game anthem. Kotoni Staggs celebrates a try against the Cook Islands. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images The Brisbane centre received the backing of Broncos teammate Patrick Carrigan for his stance. Staggs, who has won nine caps for Australia since his debut in 2023, said: “I’m a proud Wirajudri boy and I’m proud of who I am and where I come from and me not singing an anthem doesn’t mean that I’m not grateful.

“I still love wearing that jersey, when the anthem is getting played you look around and get emotional. Kotoni Staggs celebrates his try. Getty Images “But me not singing, it’s a whole different meaning to that and that’s just me.” Staggs said his position on singing Advance Australia Fair came from a position of wanting to honour his ancestors. “Obviously in the past and what happened back in the day I’ve just learned from that,” Staggs said.

“You also talk to your elders from back home and grandparents and stuff like and [understand] what they had to go through, it’s more of a respect for my elders and my family. “I’m a proud Australian as well but at the end of the day it’s just something that I’ve lived by, and I’ve got no harm in it. It doesn’t take anything away from the jersey I wear.” Criticism of Staggs and other Indigenous Kangaroos stars, including Latrell Mitchell, is nothing new. Former Australian Test coach Mal Meninga previously defended players for their firm stance on the matter. Carrigan said athletes should have the right to stand up for what they believe in.

“As sports people there’s a focus on us as role models but it probably points to a greater conversation for us to have as a society outside of football,” Carrigan said. title: ‘Sad and devastated’: Canva cuts hit staff and Australian tech overall
text:
Advertisement

Analysis TechnologySoftware ‘Sad and devastated’: Canva cuts hit staff and Australian tech overall David Swan November 4, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Dunja Popovs woke up on Wednesday to the news that she was one of the 22 per cent of design software maker Canva’s workers losing their job. “Truthfully, I am sad and devastated, but I’m also extremely grateful that I ever had the opportunity in the first place,” Popovs, who led a team of content designers at Canva, wrote on LinkedIn. Her plan for now is “a whole lot of gardening”, then to start hunting for a new job. Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams at the Canva Create conference in Los Angeles in April. Canva chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Wednesday that 1271 people would be affected by a restructuring, aimed at resetting the business after growth started to slow this year.

Advertisement

Some will lose their jobs. Others will be asked to relocate or will find their roles rewritten. The timing was brutal: the news arrived a day after the Reserve Bank lifted rates to an 18-year-high. Anyone who has tried to get hired in tech knows not much happens between now and Australia Day. The news took me back to April, when I saw Canva close its biggest product launch ever in a Los Angeles football stadium with engineers in gold plastic crowns playing Ode to Joy on instruments that included a rubber duck. I asked co-founder Cliff Obrecht the question every Australian tech boss was getting that month. Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra were cutting thousands of jobs, much of it put down to AI. Was Canva next? The answer was definitive. “We do not have to do layoffs, and we don’t have any plans to do layoffs,” Obrecht said. Canva’s headcount growth had slowed from 50 per cent a year to under 5 per cent, and he pitched that as the grown-up alternative to what everyone else was doing. “Rather than this gas-on, hit-reverse, lay-off kind of mentality,” he said, “we’ve seen this coming, and we’ve just eased our foot off the accelerator.”

Advertisement

I believed him, and so did plenty of the people who got the email on Wednesday. One departing engineer described it as the “grim reaper of the tech world” arriving “a lot sooner than I thought it ever would”. Most staff were surprised, he said. To be fair to Obrecht, I think he meant every word. Canva had been profitable for nine straight years and had more than $US1.5 billion ($2.2 billion) in the bank. It had never needed to do major layoffs. Then the numbers turned, in large part due to the rapid rise of AI. In August, I reported that Canva had slowed that product launch because AI bills were eating its margins. Canva co-founder Cliff Obrecht. Peter Rae “Historically, the cost to create a design cost us essentially nothing,” Obrecht said in August. “The cost of goods to serve a user has gone from cents per month to many, many more cents.”

Advertisement

Canva’s internal valuation of its business, used to price staff shares, tumbled as a result, and Perkins’ email confirmed growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. She didn’t link the cuts directly to AI, but others are less sure the threat is temporary. Adam Barty, who runs Melbourne AI agency Revium, says it’s “pretty hard not to view AI as an existential threat to Canva’s core business model”, which is to give people who aren’t designers an easy way to make things free and convert enough of them into paying subscribers. Some long-term users have moved their slideshows and social posts to AI chatbots and barely open Canva anymore. For a decade, Canva has been the most successful story in Australian tech: a 19-year-old in Perth and her boyfriend, more than 100 investor rejections, then the most valuable start-up this country has produced. Its co-founders are now billionaires and every pitch deck in Surry Hills borrowed a little of its shine. Canva’s Cliff Orbrecht (left), Cameron Adams and Melanie Perkins. Getty

Advertisement

This setback is grim news for staff, but also for Australia’s venture capital sector, which has effectively been propped up by Canva’s outsized success. Related Article Updated

Software Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history Venture capital firm Blackbird owns about 10 per cent of Canva, and it has been a huge success for the firm until now. Airtree first invested in 2014 and has asked its own investors to keep its fund open until 2028 in the hope of a payday. Behind both firms sit wealthy families, endowments and super funds. If Canva’s value keeps sliding, so does the case that backing Australian start-ups is a sound use of retirement savings. Where things go from here is an open question, as is Canva’s very survival over the long term. An IPO looks further off than ever. A sale to a global tech giant near Canva’s current value could be an option and would be one of the biggest software deals ever done.

Advertisement

But there’s always a silver lining. When Google shut its Wave project (an attempt to build a social media platform for users to collaborate) in Sydney in 2010, a crop of talented engineers went looking for something new. One of them was Cameron Adams, who became Canva’s third co-founder. Canva is about to release a much bigger crop, with $US10,000 grants for anyone who wants to start their own business. If even a handful of those are successful, then Australian tech’s next big story started on Wednesday. David Swan travelled to Los Angeles in April with the support of Canva. Football Australia is eager to have Tony Popovic’s future as Socceroos coach resolved before Christmas, but football boss Heather Garriock has warned that other candidates are “knocking at the door” as negotiations continue over a contract extension. Garriock, FA’s executive director of football and deputy CEO, told this masthead discussions were already under way with Popovic’s agent, Frank Trimboli, after the postponement of January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia threw the federation’s coaching plans into disarray. Loading Popovic turned down a four-year extension on the eve of the World Cup in favour of a short-term deal – partly because, as Garriock revealed last month on the Suited & Booted podcast, they could not reach agreement over financial terms. Garriock confirmed Popovic’s current contract actually expires in March, and does not automatically extend because the Asian Cup has been postponed by nearly 12 months. The tournament will now kick off on December 23, 2027 and run through to January 21, 2028, subject to FIFA approval.

Advertisement

FA’s immediate preference, Garriock said, is to retain Popovic at least until the end of the rescheduled Asian Cup – even if that means he could be in the dugout in September, when Australia’s qualification campaign for the 2030 FIFA World Cup begins, without any guarantee he would see it through. “We’ve already been speaking, even before this. That’s ongoing at the moment,” Garriock told this masthead. Socceroos coach Tony Popovic. Dominic Lorrimer “We need to do what’s best for both Football Australia and Tony, and they’re the discussions that we’re having at the moment. Our first priority is making sure that we both are happy with an extension for the Asian Cup. “We’ve got people knocking on our door, but we need to give Tony the best opportunity, because he’s actually delivered and done the business for Football Australia, he’s prepared the players amazingly well, and for us to give him the best opportunity to win a trophy for the Socceroos … it’s only fair.”

Advertisement

Garriock praised Popovic for the way he has strengthened the Socceroos’ brand, bolstered the national team’s player depth and re-established “accountability” for the Australian jersey. She also said his tenure – with Popovic having replaced Graham Arnold at short notice two years ago, at a precarious juncture in World Cup qualifying – showed changing coaches mid-cycle was not an impediment to success. Football Australia executive director of football and deputy CEO, Heather Garriock. Getty Images for Football Australia “Tony’s demonstrated that it’s not an absolute must,” she said. Popovic’s four-year contract offer from FA was not publicly known until he revealed it unprompted in a press conference in September – but he did not mention remuneration being a factor behind his decision to knock it back, simply saying a short-term renewal gave both parties flexibility to consider their positions after the Asian Cup.

Advertisement

Popovic also made clear at the time that he would be comfortable walking away from the national team after the Asian Cup, irrespective of the team’s performance, and that his own job security was not important to him. “I know the legacy that I’ll leave behind,” he said. “And if it’s someone else that takes it forward, that’s fine.” Asked about her comments on the podcast that “it came down to money”, Garriock said FA were restricted in what they could offer any national team coach. “We’re the governing body, and we need to live within our means,” she said. “We need to future-proof and make sure our business is sustainable. Unfortunately, we can’t pay what a club pays … it’s a vastly different role and an expectation to being paid at club level.”

Advertisement

The challenge with a 12-month extension for Popovic is that FA could miss out on other coaches who will become available in the coming months – in particular, Kevin Muscat, who is coming out of contract with Chinese club Shanghai Port at the end of the year and would be receptive to discussions over the Socceroos job if Popovic did not continue, sources said. “I think we need to get this put away by Christmas,” Garriock said. Other nations face similar dilemmas. Graham Arnold’s short-term contract with Iraq was also due to expire after the Asian Cup, while Japan had already announced that Hajime Moriyasu would hand over to Go Oiwa after the tournament. Both federations, like Australia, must now revisit their plans. Meanwhile, Popovic is set to unveil his squad on Friday for this month’s friendlies in the Middle East against Qatar and Jordan, which were to be their final warm-up games before the Asian Cup, and could yet be his final matches in charge of the Socceroos. Despite the uncertainty over the coaching position, Garriock said those would still be important fixtures to prepare the team for what lies ahead, including the new World Cup qualifying campaign.

Advertisement

Related Article Asian Cup Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos facing massive Popovic dilemma Some players, however, have expressed discomfort about the prospect of travelling to the region, according to sources close to the team, due to the deteriorating security situation. Garriock said any player would be excused from this window without any future repercussions if they chose not to go for those reasons. “It’s normal for both staff and players to be hesitant to want to travel to the Middle East at the moment,” she said. “However, we’ve got the best intelligence on the ground, and we wouldn’t put the players or staff at risk. It’s a matter for the players to decide whether they want to travel, and we’ll support their decision, both the players and staff – and it certainly won’t have an impact on selection going forward.”

text:

If you still have a David Jones gift card, now might be a good time to cash it in before the retailer’s board meets this evening and turns your voucher into the equivalent of a losing Melbourne Cup ticket. The board meeting is expected to perform last rites on what is left of the failing 188-year-old department store operator and put the company into voluntary administration. David Jones has run out of options after landlords refused a rescue deal for the department store operator. Ruby Alexander David Jones has run out of options and will need the protection of corporate undertakers to keep landlords and lenders at bay. But it won’t last long. Its major lender, Hilco Capital, will then appoint its own receiver to restructure and sell the business, and try to recoup its money.

Advertisement

That will involve drastic surgery to reduce the storied department store chain to a more modest store footprint – with lower rents – so that it just might remain viable. No one needs reminding how tough a job this will be. And not just based on the Reserve Bank’s latest interest rate rise this week. When the retailer’s payment troubles extended to its landlords last month, the writing was on the wall. Department stores globally have been under major pressure from online shopping, smaller and more nimble physical rivals and diminishing foot traffic as more people work from home. The headwinds have led to financial troubles, closures and bankruptcies across the globe, including at iconic Saks Fifth Avenue in New York. The worst cost-of-living crisis in decades may just be the final straw.

Advertisement

Research from MST Marquee published this week flagged a dozen store closures for David Jones, which would cost thousands of staff their jobs in the lead-up to Christmas. Related Article Updated

Retail On knife’s edge: David Jones could appoint administrators by Thursday The temptation would be to blame Anchorage Capital, the private equity firm that took the keys to the famous Australian department store more than three years ago. Who can forget the role Anchorage played in selling electronics group Dick Smith to the Australian public in 2013 at a massive profit, just a year after acquiring the business from Woolworths? Dick Smith collapsed in 2016. The fact that Anchorage paid just $100 million for David Jones in 2023 says plenty about how thin the veneer of viability was already by that stage.

Advertisement

Woolworths South Africa had spent $2.1 billion acquiring the struggling retailer in 2014, but its ownership was marred by quick CEO turnover and massive writedowns of a business clearly in decline. More significantly, Woolworths sold off David Jones’s property assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars to help ease the financial pain. This included the flagship Sydney and Melbourne stores. What Anchorage acquired for $100 million was a brand name, a turnaround plan and massive lease liabilities for stores that David Jones no longer owned. “The business is positioned as a premium and luxury offering with complementary services across fashion and beauty,” Anchorage said when it sealed the deal in 2023. David Jones was already implementing plans to spend $250 million on revamping its stores, its loyalty program, digital presence and customer relationship systems to boost sales and better compete with online retailers and luxury brands going direct to consumers.

Advertisement

That revamp was completed late last year, but it was not enough to turn the tide. Related Article Opinion

Retail How one David Jones supplier got paid when the others didn’t Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Suppliers have been ending exclusive deals with David Jones and defecting to rival Myer. And the group hit a cash crunch. By January, suppliers started complaining of delayed payment terms. In March, David Jones was late paying some suppliers and was pushing them all towards 60-day payment terms. In effect, it was using suppliers as a de facto bank, using proceeds from the sale of their goods for extended amounts of time before paying its bills.

Advertisement

“We note that recent media commentary is best characterised as misinformed – like many businesses, David Jones is adjusting some operational processes to best position the business for sustainable, long-term growth,” a spokesperson for Anchorage said at the time. When the retailer’s payment troubles extended to its landlords last month, the writing was on the wall for its continued survival. title: In Beijing, Mbappé’s face still spruiks drinks amid broadcast blackout
text:
