Beijing: On the streets of Beijing, the French footballer Kylian Mbappé’s face still peeks out from the chilled drinks cabinets of China Post-owned newsstands. From behind the glass fridge doors, a smiling Mbappé graces bottles of peach-flavoured sport drinks that promise to quench thirst and replenish electrolytes. They are clearly visible to passers-by, with front-row billing alongside bottles of green tea, energy drinks and Coca-Cola. A kiosk in Beijing’s Chaoyang district sells the Mbappé-promoted sports drink after the Real Madrid star was forced to apologise for remarks about a meme comparing him to Mao Zedong. Lisa Visentin But Mbappé’s face was absent from Chinese televisions this past weekend. Fans who wanted to see him slot an 11th-minute penalty against Racing Santander in the Spanish LaLiga match on Sunday were denied the chance. China’s state broadcaster CCTV did not air the match, despite a broadcast deal with LaLiga, Spain’s professional soccer league, amid an ongoing fallout over the Real Madrid star’s perceived slight against China’s founding leader Mao Zedong. The great cancellation has not yet trickled down to street vendors.

Advertisement

A short walk through the inner suburbs of Beijing’s Chaoyang district revealed at least three kiosks and one supermarket were stocking the Mbappé-endorsed drink this week, after beverage giant Dongpeng joined several other Chinese companies in severing promotional deals with the star. “I only saw the news about this in passing, so I don’t know exactly what he [Mbappé] said,” said 56-year-old Shi, who manages one China Post-owned street kiosk. She had restocked her drinks cabinet with more Mbappé drinks since the weekend but was not sure whether the supplier would send more once this stock was sold. Kylian Mbappe upset some Chinese people by laughing at a meme depicting him as Mao Zedong. Jamie Brown However, her views on Mao help explain the genesis of the outrage, even as many Chinese people remain in the dark about the details of Mbappé’s remarks, which have been blocked by government censors, deemed too egregious to be broadcast to the masses.

Advertisement

“As a Chinese person, I grew up listening to Chairman Mao’s songs and quotations. My love and affection for Chairman Mao are beyond question,” Shi said. ‘My feelings for Chairman Mao are not something I can express in words; it’s something ingrained in my bones.’ Shi, Beijing kiosk manager “I’m almost 60 now. It may be different for younger generation today. My feelings for Chairman Mao are not something I can express in words; it’s something ingrained in my bones.” At another kiosk a few hundreds metres away, the operators also had no knowledge of the Mbappé scandal and no one had advised them to stop selling the Mbappé-promoted drinks, they said. “We don’t know about it,” said the kiosk manager, who declined to give his name, while his colleague pulled out her phone to search the news. “These are matters of state. I’m not interested in that. All I care about is whether I can make any money at my shop today. National affairs are for the state to handle. They don’t have much to do with ordinary people like us.”

Advertisement

A 1960s poster of Mao Zedong. Getty Images The Real Madrid striker was forced to issue an apology last week for a months-old interview in which he laughed at a meme depicting him as “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. Real Madrid and LaLiga president Javier Tebas also issued apologies. Related Article Inside China ‘Not accepted. Not forgiven!!’ : French superstar’s ‘dictator Mao’ meme ignites fury in China The meme in question showed Mbappé’s face photoshopped onto Mao’s body — one of many viral memes that depict the footballer as different dictators from history, in a joke that taps into his commanding presence inside teams. Mao, who led China from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains widely revered by many in China. He is credited for ending China’s domination by imperialist forces and heralding its independence.

Advertisement

Discussion of his legacy is tightly controlled by Chinese authorities, especially when it comes to the catastrophic impact of the industrialisation campaign known as the Great Leap Forward in the late 1950s and early ’60s, and the ensuing famine that killed millions of people, and the Cultural Revolution from 1966 which triggered widespread violence and bloodshed. The scandal has exposed the paradox of the Chinese censorship system that fanned the flames of outrage while blocking the original content that would allow citizens to reach their own verdict, triggering some to go looking for answers. ‘What exactly did Mbappe do? I can’t find anything about it.’ Weibo post To access the video of Mbappé’s interview, Chinese citizens need to use a virtual private network (VPN) to jump the Great Firewall that blocks them from accessing the Western internet, an act that is technically prohibited in China. Kylian Mbappe celebrates after scoring his side’s opening goal during a Spanish La Liga soccer match in Spain, Sunday on October 25, 2026. AP

Advertisement

On social media, some people demanded that vendors cover up Mbappé’s face on the drinks packaging; others were perplexed about the origins of the scandal. “What exactly did Mbappe do? I can’t find anything about it,” one person posted on Chinese microblogging site Weibo. “Just search for it on the internet beyond China’s firewall and you’ll find it. They don’t let you see it on the Chinese internet...,” another user responded. It remains unclear when the broadcast blackout will end and Real Madrid games will be aired again in China. Government-owned China Media Group (CMG) said last week that “Mbappé’s outrageous remarks have harmed the Chinese people, crossed a line and exceeded the scope of freedom of speech”.

title: 'They don't need it': Trump signals early end to $5.4 billion Israel military aid deal
text:
IN BRIEF Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu is "fine" with the $5.4 billion in annual aid ending, Donald Trump has said.

US support for Israel became a divisive issue for voters ahead of the midterm elections.

United States President Donald Trump has appeared to announce that the US will end its annual US$3.8 billion ($5.4 billion) in aid to Israel.

His comments come the day of the midterm elections, in which support for Israel has been a contentious issue.

"We give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said during a phone interview with Fox News on Wednesday.

Trump said Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "fine" with the decision to end the aid.

Under the deal, Israel receives financial assistance for the purchase of around $US3.8 billion in weapons a year.

"Now, we'll help Israel if they need it," Trump said.

"Israel is a very thriving country. They don't need it."

The announcement came as Americans voted in crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's presidency, and after parliamentary elections in Israel — which did not produce a clear winner.

Since its founding in 1948, Israel has received more than US$300 billion ($430 billion), adjusted for inflation, in US economic and military assistance, according to the US-based Council on Foreign Relations, far more than any other country in that time period.

Netanyahu has in the past expressed a desire to end Israel's dependence on US aid. In May, he told US broadcaster CBS that he wanted to reduce US support to zero.

Wednesday's announcement drew backlash from Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who said it showed that Netanyahu must go.

"The fact that Israel's defence establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media at the same time as the Israeli public shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is," Eisenkot said in a statement.

"He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced."

It was not immediately clear when the US aid to Israel would actually end.

US divided over Israeli alliance

The US' role in the conflict in Gaza has created deep divisions within the country, with polls showing a growing number of Americans in favour of cutting aid to Israel.

The announcement also comes amid an eight-month war against Iran, with Trump confirming on Tuesday that the US military had carried out new strikes there.

Trump cited criticism from leftist Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the US Senate after harnessing popular discontent and anti-Israel sentiment, as part of the reasoning behind the decision to end the aid package.

"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it? It's a bad talking point," Trump said on Fox, referring to the aid for Israel.

READ MORE Who is Abdul El-Sayed? The Michigan doctor who wants to lead the left to the US Senate

The debate over support for Israel, which divides both Democrats and Republicans, is raging in El-Sayed's home state of Michigan, where there is a large Muslim community.

If he wins, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate. He has been a vocal critic of the US alliance with Israel, calling for a halt to aid to the country.

His criticism of Israel was one factor behind Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens' — El-Sayed's main rival in the party's primary — endorsing his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers — illustrating divisions within the party on the issue.

title: A GLP-1 weight loss pill has been approved in Australia. Here's what we know
text:
IN BRIEF The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved the use of the Wegovy tablet in Australia.

The eligibility for Australians accessing subsidised GLP-1 medication remains limited.

Australians wanting to take weight-loss drugs will no longer have to inject themselves, with the first daily tablet version now medically approved.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) cleared various doses of the Wegovy tablet, made by Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, on Tuesday.

Previously, Australians had to take the GLP-1 weight-loss drug in the form of a weekly injection.

The daily tablet form of the appetite-suppressing medication was approved for use in the UK in June and in the US late last year.

Novo Nordisk said it expected the pill would be available in Australia before the end of the year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We will share confirmed availability timing as soon as we can," a spokesperson said.

Endocrinologist John Wentworth welcomed the news, saying it would make the drug easier for patients to take.

He said trial data indicated the tablet version of the drug worked just as well as the jabs.

He told ABC News Breakfast that many individuals prefer to avoid self-injecting, particularly when travelling.

"People don't like injecting themselves ... they're going on a holiday," he said.

"So instead of taking the needles, they'll transition onto the tablets and then come back."

How much will the medication cost, and will it be subsidised?

The TGA said it had approved the drug for weight management and for reducing the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, like stroke or heart attack, in eligible adults.

The tablets have been approved in 1.5mg, 4mg, 9mg and 25mg strengths, and added to the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods.

The price of the pill version of the drugs has not been announced, but the injectables are not on Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, except for those with Type 2 Diabetes.

As a result, about 400,000 Australians currently pay up to $5,000 a year to access Wegovy, Ozempic and other GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.

The federal government is currently in negotiations with the manufacturer to bring Wegovy onto the scheme for a small cohort of extra patients, which would bring the price down to $25 per script or $7.70 for concession card holders.

The approval would also make the drug cheaper and more accessible, Wentworth said.

"When the price comes down, we will be treating these just as we treat a blood pressure or a cholesterol medication because they have such powerful benefits to keep us well for longer."

title: 'A shameful chapter of history': King Charles withholds apology for slavery in the Caribbean
text:
Key Points The Commonwealth summit gathered 56 members states to Antigua to meet with the King.

Buckingham Palace has repeatedly ruled out financial reparations over its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

King Charles has told Commonwealth leaders the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow", but did not offer an apology.

In his address to presidents and prime ministers at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua, Charles said his commitment was growing to find ways to "address the wrongs of the past with action for the future".

The ‌run-up to the gathering of the 56 member states, which comprise mostly former British colonies, has been dominated by talk of whether Britain should apologise or pay reparations for the role it played in the transatlantic slave trade.

He delivered his speech on Tuesday against the background of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing a change in long-established government policy and making an offer of talks on a slavery apology but not financial reparations.

"Our history inspires us, can appal us, yet it can always teach us. We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can, however, learn from the past," he said.

"The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth ... that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.

"And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role.

"The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

Charles also told the gathering of world leaders: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know."

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures — the good they did as well as the wrongs."

Calls for an apology and reparations from the UK have been growing in recent years and St Lucia's Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, chairman of the 15-member Caribbean Community, has reportedly said the economic and political bloc was "ready to engage" in the structured dialogue Burnham offered.

Burnham has also gone further than his predecessors by saying he was open to Britain apologising for slavery and officials were holding talks with national ‌leaders at the summit to discuss what form that could take.

title: Tickets, flights and protein: Meet the winners of Australia's 'Shonky' Awards
text:
IN BRIEF Ticketek, Ticketmaster, Virgin and Hisense are some of the products and services Choice has named in its annual 'shonky' awards.

The 'awards', which call out products the organisation deems to be dodgy, have been running for more than two decades.

Major ticket merchants are accused of twisting the knife in Australians already battling a cost of living crisis.

On Wednesday, Consumer advocacy group Choice revealed its annual Shonky Award winners, calling out the products and services it deems the most dodgy.

Ticketek and Ticketmaster featured on the list for what the group labelled as gouging customers with sneaky tactics.

Both merchants allow dynamic pricing schemes, through which ticket costs can rise during sale periods.

Earlier this year, Ticketek earned the ire of John Farnham fans, who criticised fluctuating prices for tickets to his September tribute concert.

About 7 per cent of tickets were affected by variable pricing for the Farnham tribute.

title: The Australian territory where online forms, banks and services don't always work
text:
Norfolk Island is, legally speaking, part of Australia. But running a business in this remote Pacific territory, home to around 2,100 residents, can be very different from on the mainland.

Government forms can reject local telephone numbers and banking services can be difficult to access. Even routine changes to internet services can leave businesses disconnected.

This speaks to its geographic challenges — Norfolk lies some 1,500km from the Australian mainland — as well as some unique complexities stemming from its unusual political and administrative history.

In 1856, following the closure of its British penal settlements, Norfolk became home to descendants of the HMS Bounty mutineers and Tahitians from Pitcairn Island. The Pitcairn community brought its own traditions and governing practices, which helped shape Norfolk’s distinctive identity long before it became an Australian territory in 1914.

Norfolk gained a substantial degree of self-government in 1979, before Canberra abolished the arrangement in 2015. Australian taxation, employment laws, Medicare and social security followed, bringing benefits alongside new obligations. The island’s regional council has been under administration since 2021, while disputes over its governance continue.

Now, a new survey of Norfolk Island businesses examines the difficulties they face, from freight and insurance costs to navigating laws and commercial systems designed for mainland Australia.

An unusual economy, under pressure

The Business Council of Norfolk Island received responses from 103 of 239 businesses contacted, with nearly half reporting worsening conditions over the past year. Long-established businesses were particularly affected, with 27 of 42 reporting deterioration, compared with four of 21 established in the past three years.

Freight was the biggest concern, identified by 70 per cent of respondents who answered the question, followed by insurance at 45 per cent. Other concerns included visitor spending, telecommunications and air services.

Norfolk has no conventional deep-water port. Cargo ships anchor offshore while cranes lower goods into smaller vessels, known as lighters. These shuttle to the pier, where freight is lifted ashore. Heavy seas can interrupt unloading, while biosecurity requirements complicate imports.

READ MORE Why one tiny island's Census is about much more than numbers

New Commonwealth-funded cargo-transfer vessels have been introduced, but freight still requires specialised handling. Changes to shipping connections with New Zealand have complicated supply arrangements, while air freight provides a more frequent but expensive alternative.

Businesses must plan orders around shipping schedules, allow for delays and find alternative supplies when deliveries are disrupted. While some costs are unavoidable, managing these disruptions takes considerable time and effort. Other difficulties arise from government and commercial systems that don’t accommodate the island’s circumstances.

Norfolk’s five-digit telephone numbers don’t always fit online forms designed for mainland Australia. A 2023 parliamentary inquiry heard of online forms rejecting local numbers, including during Australian Business Number applications.

Norfolk Island is home to around 2,100 residents. Source: Getty / Oliver Strewe

Two-factor authentication creates further problems when banking and software services cannot send verification codes to local numbers. Some businesses maintain separate Australian mobile services simply to access everyday services.

Even the island’s postcode, 2899, is assigned to New South Wales by Australia Post, although Norfolk is legally an external territory, creating confusion in commercial systems.

Last month, local users reported Starlink services being suspended following an apparent change in how the company recognised service locations, disrupting businesses reliant on satellite internet.

The incident illustrates how a seemingly minor change in a global provider’s systems can have significant consequences for an isolated community, leaving local businesses to resolve problems they had no part in creating.

The burden of changing rules

Norfolk’s older businesses developed their practices and commercial relationships under different taxation, employment and administrative arrangements. Newer enterprises have operated within the post-2016 system from the outset.

Established businesses may therefore face additional costs adapting longstanding arrangements to newer requirements. This could help explain why older businesses reported worsening conditions more often, although sector, size and market conditions may also play a part.

Norfolk’s legal arrangements add another complication. Businesses operate under a mixture of Commonwealth law, selected state legislation and laws retained from the former Norfolk government. Determining which requirements apply can require specialist advice that’s difficult to obtain locally.

The latest survey found a similar divide between employers and sole operators. Among respondents, 41 per cent of businesses with employees reported adverse effects from laws, regulations or policies, compared with 7 per cent of sole operators.

Norfolk Island is located around 1,500km off the coast of Australia.

Employers must manage payroll, workplace conditions, safety and reporting obligations. These provide important protections, but compliance requires time, resources and expertise that can be difficult to access on the island.

My current research examines how Norfolk Island businesses have adapted to the governance changes introduced a decade ago.

Businesses must plan around uncertain freight deliveries, navigate overlapping legal requirements and find ways to use digital systems that don’t always recognise where they operate. These efforts keep businesses running, but take time and money away from serving customers, improving services and growing their operations.

Norfolk Island illustrates a problem facing other small and remote communities. National and global systems can work efficiently for millions of people while leaving those outside their assumptions to resolve the exceptions themselves.

For Norfolk’s businesses, the difficulty is not simply operating far from the mainland, but the additional time and resources needed to make those systems work.

Rod McNaughton is a professor of entrepreneurship at the University of Auckland, Waipapa Taumata Rau. He received funding for this research from Juncture: Dialogues on Inclusive Capitalism, a research centre within the University of Auckland Business School.

title: See the full list: The jobs Australian employers are struggling most to fill
text:
In Brief New data shows workforce shortages continue to persist in a variety of industries.

Nearly 280 occupations are in shortage across the country, representing 27 per cent of those assessed.

Want to get into horse breeding? Are you a pyschotherapist or a landscape designer? These are just three occupations newly listed as in shortage this year by a government agency.

Other occupations, such as roof tiler, gas fitter, mining engineer, psychologist and podiatrist, have consistently been listed as in shortage each year since 2021.

They are just some of the 127 occupations that have consistently faced worker shortages since 2021. They broadly fall into the field of technicians and trade workers and professionals.

Data from Jobs and Skills Australia shows despite shortages continuing to ease across several fields, companies are still struggling to fill many roles across a variety of industries. Twenty-eight new occupations were in shortage this year, spread across health, science, trades and operations. Some, such as student services adviser and exercise physiologist, are only listed as being in shortage in regional areas.

While technicians and trade workers make up the largest proportion of persistent shortages, other impacted roles tend to be in construction, early childhood education, engineering, health, and science.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government body suggests three key factors are contributing to shortages: constraints on the supply of potential workers, a lack of suitable applicants and retention issues.

Occupations in shortage tend to have longer vacancy durations and lower rates of being filled.

In industries experiencing a shortage, recruiters tended to identify half as many qualified and suitable candidates. On average, a job offered in an occupation with a shortage received six qualified applicants, and three suitable ones, compared to roles in non-shortage fields which had 13 qualified candidates and six suitable people for the position.

Which occupations are in shortage?

In this year's report, 279 occupations are in shortage across the country, representing 27 per cent of those assessed. The government body says this is down from the peak in 2023, when 36 per cent of assessed roles were in shortage.

Here are the occupations impacted.

How do shortages get addressed?

Professor Larissa Bamberry, a professor of employment and gender relations at the Charles Sturt University School of Business, said discussions around workforce issues tend to use familiar narratives such as "we can't get people, we can't keep people, there aren't enough skilled workers".

"All those things can be true, but one of the most important things I've learnt from working with regional employers and communities is that workforce problems are rarely one single problem," she told SBS News.

"It's usually a mixture of a number of factors tangled together, and they need quite different policy responses."

READ MORE Not just call centres: The skilled Australian jobs now moving offshore

Bamberry said it's better to consider a skills ecosystem approach to assess needs on a region-by-region basis, supported by collaboration between employers, TAFEs and universities to address concerns within that sector and region.

"We tend to go for pipeline responses, which are very much like, 'oh, we will just churn out the right number of people, and we'll hope that those people end up in the right industries and in the right locations'," she said.

"And they often don't."

Regional challenges

Employers in regional areas tend to find it harder to fill vacant roles. In regional areas, 15 occupations are in shortage, decreasing from 21 last year.

Bamberry said a tailored approach allowed policy responses to better address the needs of potential applicants.

Potential issues range from access to public transport, roads, transportation and internet service, through to the distance to education facilities or the demographics of the community.

Instead, she proposes tailoring "the people that we train, the places where we train them, and the industries that we train for".

READ MORE The growing issue that could make migrating to Australia less attractive

In some areas, there may be enough interested workers, but the skills needed for their roles continue to change.

"There's a lot of people who have the knowledge they need for farming, but don't necessarily have the data analysis, sort of technical skills that are required in modern farming these days because we've got AI and we've got so much technological change happening so rapidly," Bamberry said.

The way to fill these roles may be to connect people to the upskilling they seek, rather than increasing the number of potential workers more generally.

"You wouldn't necessarily want to start an international migration program, for example, around horse breeding, but you might have somebody who's got an interest in horse breeding who is in the particular location but hasn't got the particular skills that they need."

title: 'Heartbroken': Spanish footballer dies after collision during match
text:
In brief Jesús de Miguel was hospitalised after an incident during a Spanish second-division match on Monday.

His club, CD Tenerife, announced his "tragic passing" on Tuesday.

A 30-year-old footballer has died a day after colliding with an opponent during a Spanish second-division match, his club said on Tuesday.

Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel died after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match, CD Tenerife said.

"Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing of Jesús de Miguel Alameda," the club said.

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness."

De Miguel was challenging for the ball during a home game on Monday when he was struck in the chest by Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during the final minutes at Estadio Heliodoro Rodríguez López.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was suspended in the 108th minute.

He lay motionless as players from both teams desperately signalled for medical assistance. Owono was shown a straight red card.

Medical staff treated the player on the pitch for more than five minutes before he was taken to hospital by ambulance.

Tenerife said in a statement that De Miguel died at 8am (local time) on Tuesday. The club, located on Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken".

De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

Tributes flow in

Football clubs across Spain, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, have led tributes following the news of the death.

"Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times," Barcelona said in a statement.

Real Madrid also expressed their condolences, stating: "Real Madrid wishes to express its condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones."

Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences.

"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.

The Spanish football federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina match to be held later on Tuesday.

title: Asian Cup postponed for 11 months due to conflict in the Middle East
text:
In brief Saudi Arabia's Asian Cup has been pushed back by nearly a year due to the war in the Middle East.

The delayed tournament could have ramifications for Socceroos coach Tony Popovic.

The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed as a result of the conflict in the Middle East.

After a month of speculation following the airport attack on Riyadh's international airport, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) confirmed on Tuesday that the tournament had been pushed back 11 months.

The rescheduled tournament is expected to kick off in the 2027 Christmas break with a 23 December start date leading up to a 21 January 2028 final.

"The organising committee for AFC Asian Cup approved rescheduling the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," the AFC said in a statement.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

title: RBA's Cup Day call takes rates to 18-year high; board divided over decision — as it happened
text:
The RBA governor is talking

RBA governor Michele Bullock says she knows this was not the news many Australians wanted, but "it's what's needed to get inflation down".

"Inflation is too high and our forecasts suggest it will stay higher for longer," she said at a press conference.

"Part of the reason for inflation staying higher for longer is global oil prices. However, I want to be very clear that we are not tightening monetary policy because of the direct impact of oil prices on inflation."

She noted that rate hikes began before the start of the war in Iran.

"Monetary policy cannot impact global oil prices. Rather, the tightening in monetary policy is to address domestic capacity pressures. These were evident before the rise in oil prices, which is why the board started to increase the cash rate in February this year."

"We now think that those pressures were greater and contributed more to inflation than we judged before."

She said that Australians with mortgages are not the only ones dealing with the higher cost of living.

"I understand that today's decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments, but households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough," she said.

"If high inflation were allowed to become entrenched, interest rates would ultimately need to stay higher for longer, with greater risks for economic growth and jobs."

— Josie Harvey

title: UK adventurer embraces mother after completing 28-year trek around the world
text:
In brief Bushby set out from Chile in 1998 and walked 50,000km across four continents and 30 countries to get home.

The 57-year-old said he expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys.

British adventurer Karl Bushby enjoyed an emotional reunion with his mother and family on Monday as he arrived back home after a 28-year, 50,000-km trek from South America, crossing four continents on foot.

Cheers erupted as the 57-year-old former paratrooper was greeted in the street outside his mother's house in the north-eastern UK port city of Hull.

Bushby, who set off on his odyssey from Chile in 1998, had two golden rules for his journey — avoid all forms of transport to advance and not return until he completed his challenge.

He was met in the centre of Hull by a crowd of up to 1,000 cheering people before being reunited with his mother, Angela, 36-year-old son Adam and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

Speaking after the reunion, Bushby paid tribute to the kindness of the strangers he had met, from hotel owners to the "poorest of the poor" who had given him bowls of rice and something to drink along the way.

"And that would happen throughout the world," he said, adding that the world had been his "support network".

'Indiana Jones' moments

The route back to his home city has taken him across the Americas, across the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, and then through parts of Central Asia and Europe, covering jungles, mountains, and deserts.

The journey had been full of logistical headaches and scary "Indiana Jones" and "I think I'm going to die moments", he told reporters.

Bushby had already been applauded on Sunday as he crossed the iconic Humber Bridge near Hull in thick mist, ahead of his final push into the city centre and then on to his mother's home where he grew up.

Karl Bushby in Nevada in the United States in 2003. Source: PA / tiktok.com/@karlcbushby

"So many people have followed Karl on his epic journey. We have all felt inspired by his spirit, tenacity and dogged determination," Hull mayor Maria Coward said ahead of his arrival.

"It's quite emotional. I'm proud of him and what he's done. What an achievement," neighbour Laura Chaplin, 47, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency as he returned home.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson said it was "an extraordinary achievement and the prime minister welcomes him back to the UK".

Challenges met

Bushby began his adventure aged 29, after his marriage broke down and his wife returned to Northern Ireland with their son.

He was forced to pause the journey several times, including when Moscow refused him a visa. The 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic caused other hold-ups.

At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably at a base in Mexico, then once the situation had been resolved, he would resume from the exact spot where he had left off.

Erin Anderson, 28, a theatre marketing officer among the crowd in Hull, said she thought Bushby was "amazing".

"I've been following him for the last eight years. He's been walking for as long as I've been alive. It's brilliant."

What's next for Bushby?

Bushby swam across the Channel from France in early October to return to the UK.

Legendary German filmmaker Werner Herzog and a film crew accompanied Bushby on his homecoming, making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled Walk of Life.

The production company behind the film has been supporting Bushby's progress for the past 16 years, providing financial and logistical assistance.

Bushby said he would now be focusing on the documentary, as well as writing a book and adjusting back to normal life.

James Bushby was mobbed by well-wishers as he arrived in Hull after his 28-year trek. Source: EPA / Adam Vaughan

"I'm still in that shocked phase," he told AFP. "Over the last few days it's been the last time I've been camping in my tent ... last time spending all day on the road.

"Each one of those has been an emotional event and then walking down my childhood street into my childhood home with mother (there), that's been quite something," he said.

He added that he still had the drive for adventure but ruled out any more big walks.

"I think I'm hanging my boots up — 28 years is a good run."

title: What number should your interest rate have in front of it?
text:
IN BRIEF It's widely anticipated the RBA will raise the rate to 4.85 per cent, a fifth rise in 2026.

Experts say it's worth speaking with your bank, or shopping around for better options.

Homeowners could save big by negotiating or refinancing their mortgages, experts say, as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) prepares to decide on its cash rate on Tuesday.

It's widely anticipated the RBA will raise the rate from 4.60 per cent to 4.85 per cent. If it does, it will be the fifth rate rise of 2026, and sent interest rates to an 18-year high.

For those on variable interest rates, another hike would likely add 0.25 percentage points to their repayments, as the major banks have historically passed on the rate in full after RBA announcements.

But while a rate rise could increase mortgage pain for borrowers, it could also create an opportunity for people to negotiate their loan.

Sally Tindall is the head of data analytics at financial comparison site Canstar. She told SBS News that the best variable rate on offer was 5.89 per cent as of Tuesday morning.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's an important time to be talking to your bank," she said.

"Any kind of relief that you can get on an individual basis from your bank can help alleviate some of the pressure that the RBA is applying on you."

What is a good variable rate?

Mardy Chiah, an associate professor of finance at the University of Newcastle, told SBS News that a variable rate of around 6 per cent to 6.3 per cent for a maximum 80 per cent loan-to-value ratio (LVR) is competitive ahead of the RBA's decision.

An 80 per cent LVR means you are borrowing 80 per cent of a property's appraised value or purchase price, leaving you with a 20 per cent deposit or equity.

"If you're paying 6.5 per cent or more, it's worth shopping around or asking your bank for a better deal," he said.

Reducing your rate from 6.5 per cent to 6 per cent on a $500,000 mortgage could save you around $160 a month, or nearly $2,000 a year, assuming 30 years remaining, he explained.

Tindall said that the average variable rate sits at 6.49 per cent, so any loan at or under that figure is in the better half of loans.

A good home loan should also suit a borrower's circumstances, experts say.

Someone who values certainty might prefer a fixed interest rate, which keeps repayments stable for the fixed term. Others might prefer a variable rate, which can offer greater flexibility and the potential to benefit when rates fall.

Having a clear understanding of what you are paying for and the features attached to your loan is the most important thing.

When should borrowers negotiate or refinance?

One of the biggest mistakes borrowers can make is assuming their existing lender will automatically offer them its most competitive rate.

Banks and lenders regularly compete for new customers, so existing borrowers can sometimes end up paying more than people taking out a new mortgage.

"The bottom line is that loyalty doesn't always pay when it comes to mortgages," Chiah said.

"Banks may offer better rates to attract new customers, so existing borrowers shouldn't be afraid to ask for the same treatment."

It is also worth reviewing your loan when a fixed-rate period is about to expire, when your property has increased in value, or when you have paid down a substantial portion of your mortgage.

Barriers to refinancing

However, not everyone can refinance, as finding a new bank requires going through the institution's approval process.

A new lender won't necessarily approve a loan for someone who doesn't pass the checks and tests it puts you through.

"If you don't own 20 per cent of your home at today's values, a lender may not take you on. Some borrowers may also fail to pass serviceability tests," Tindall from Canstar explained.

Tindall described not being able to find a new bank as "mortgage prison" but said it's still worth looking at refinancing, as it could put pressure on your current bank to come to the table.

What could variable rates be after a rate hike?

An interest rate of 4.85 per cent would see any variable rate starting with a 5 "dead and buried", Tindall said.

The average variable rate would rise to 6.74 per cent in line with the RBA rise.

But there would still be some good options available, she predicted.

"The lowest variable rate could still sit below 6.20 per cent, it'll be interesting to see what the lower-cost lenders do in terms of their rates."

title: House prices are falling across Australia. But not in these places
text:
In Brief Regional home prices rose 3.1 per cent over the year, even as national values continued to fall.

The Barossa, outback SA and WA's Wheatbelt have seen the biggest increases over the year.

House prices are falling across Australia, but some regional areas are still seeing double-digit growth.

Australia's housing downturn has stretched into its seventh straight month, with national home prices falling 0.3 per cent in October.

The latest REA Group Home Price Report shows home values are now 4.3 per cent below their March peak and 1.9 per cent lower than a year ago, as higher interest rates continue to weigh on borrowing power and buyer demand.

Capital cities are leading the decline, now 5.4 per cent below their peak and 3.7 per cent lower than a year ago.

But the downturn isn't playing out evenly across the country.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While headline figures point to a broad slowdown, some regional markets continue to record strong annual growth, even as buyers pull back elsewhere.

"There's quite a bit of diversity under the headline numbers," Tim Lawless, research director at property analytics firm Cotality, told SBS News.

READ MORE Ninth life: What 30 years of housing downturns can tell us about this one

Regional home prices fell just 0.1 per cent in October and remain 3.1 per cent higher than a year ago, outperforming capital city markets despite the broader slowdown.

While regional markets have not escaped the downturn entirely, they have generally held up better than the capitals, said REA Group senior economist Eleanor Creagh.

"Regional areas in general have so far been more resilient than the capital city markets," Creagh told SBS News.

Capital cities are leading the housing drop, now 5.4 per cent below their peak and 3.7 per cent lower than a year ago. Source: SBS News

The regional hotspots bucking the trend

Several of the regions posting the largest price increases are concentrated in SA and WA.

The Barossa, Yorke and Mid North region in SA topped the annual growth rankings, with prices up 12.3 per cent over the past year.

It was followed by outback SA (11.65 per cent), outback WA (11.22 per cent) and WA's Wheatbelt region (11.02 per cent).

Tasmania's Launceston and North East region rounded out the top five, recording annual growth of 10.74 per cent.

Creagh said many of the best-performing regions shared a common advantage: affordability.

Rural regions across South Australia and Western Australia have seen some of the largest year on year price increases. Source: SBS News

"They're largely regional areas that continue to really benefit from comparative affordability advantages," Creagh said.

She pointed to regional SA, where median home values sit around $530,000, significantly lower than many regional NSW markets that have seen steeper declines.

That affordability buffer has become increasingly important as interest rates have climbed and borrowing power has fallen.

Regional markets continue to outperform

The difference between city and regional markets is stark over longer timeframes.

Regional home prices have risen 3.1 per cent over the past year, 33.9 per cent over five years and 108.4 per cent over the past decade.

By comparison, capital city prices are down 3.7 per cent over the past year and have risen 16.4 per cent over five years and 56.6 per cent over 10 years.

Regional South Australia recorded the strongest annual growth among the states, with prices rising 10.2 per cent over the year.

Western Australia followed at 8.9 per cent and Tasmania at 8.7 per cent.

Regional home prices have risen 3.1 per cent over the past year, 33.9 per cent over five years and 108.4 per cent over the past decade. Source: SBS News

Queensland recorded annual growth of 3.3 per cent, while the Northern Territory (2.4 per cent), Victoria (1.6 per cent) and NSW (1.4 per cent) posted more modest gains.

Over five years, regional WA and SA have been Australia's standout performers, with prices increasing 85.1 per cent and 84.6 per cent respectively.

Why are prices still rising?

Economists say the same factors driving prices lower nationally are helping support demand in some regional markets.

Lawless from Cotality described the current correction as "very much a demand-driven downturn", with higher borrowing costs reducing what many buyers can afford.

As household budgets come under pressure, buyers are increasingly adjusting their expectations and looking at cheaper locations.

READ MORE Why Australia's richest suburbs could be a warning for every homeowner

Creagh said many prospective buyers had effectively been pushed down the property ladder.

"We know that as interest rates have risen substantially, maximum borrowing capacities for potential buyers have also reduced substantially," she said.

"More affordable regions and property types remain an option for a broader pool of buyers, so are less impacted by interest rate rises."

Lawless said affordability pressures have become one of the dominant forces shaping the market.

"Affordability and serviceability challenges are just pushing more demand towards lower price points," he said.

'A double-edged sword'

While many regional areas are still recording growth, Creagh cautioned they are not immune from broader housing market pressures.

"High mortgage repayments and reduced purchasing power are also weighing on demand in many regional areas, but relative affordability, local conditions, stock on the market, and differing demand conditions in some regional areas mean there's much more resilience there than in capital cities."

The trend does not necessarily mean housing has become more affordable.

"Higher interest rates have reduced how much they can borrow, and the decline in home prices hasn't been enough to offset that," Creagh said.

"Better buying conditions don't mean better affordability."

— With additional reporting by Hannah Kwon.

That’s perhaps because of the fairly steady clip at which it has been launching and relaunching venues – Windsor in 2021, Paddington in 2023, a slick refurb of Windsor in April this year, and East Brisbane in June. But also, the sandwiches at these neatly branded stores are very, very good. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Related Article Popular CBD French diner closes suddenly It took this column a while to wrap its head around just how good Sunny Side is. When we first tried its sandwiches in 2023 we liked, rather than loved them. Even the signature chicken schnitty sandwich needs to be ordered the right way, which is to slip some gooey American cheese between the two slices of schnitzel, which lifts it from very good to exceptional. But the sandwiches have evolved. Most importantly, Bowers and co-owner Charline De Conto (the two are married) have made their own Hokkaido-style shokupan bread. You could argue it’s key to how good these sandwiches are. The schnitty sandwich and the eggplant sandwich. Morgan Roberts

Advertisement

The star of this triple-store setup is, no doubt, the Sunny Side classic chicken schnitty sandwich, but we don’t think it’s the most impressive. Not quite. Instead, that honour belongs to the shop’s eggplant sandwich. The Sunny Side Sandwiches eggplant sandwich “The eggplant sandwich has been there since day one,” Bowers says. “It’s one of my favourite sandwiches. It has all the best bits of the classic schnitty, but for vegetarians. “It’s funny because I often say to people, ‘It’s something that you should definitely try once,’ because once we’ve prepared it, it really has as much going on as the chicken schnitty, but in this different format.” Bowers is right. A serious amount of prep goes into this sandwich. The eggplant is sliced, bathed in salt water, and panko crumbed. And then, instead of going into the fryer, it goes into the freezer.

Advertisement

Sunny Side Sandwiches in East Brisbane. Morgan Roberts “Sometimes when you put them in a fryer at room temperature, it’s quite violent for a thin little piece of eggplant and it can break up. And when you freeze them, they actually keep their shape better,” he says. Then, once out of the fryer, it’s built the same way as the chicken schnitty: two slices of eggplant with the optional American cheese slapped in the middle; chopped iceberg lettuce dressed in Japanese mayo, dill, parsley and chives; bread and butter pickles; shokupan bread; and then a “magic sprinkle” of the shop’s signature seasoning, which features salt, nutritional yeast, Korean chilli flakes and “a few other little secret herbs and spices.” Co-owner Mack Bowers. Morgan Roberts A contender for Brisbane’s best vegetarian sanger

Advertisement

Listen, it really is up there. And, like Bowers says, it’s worth trying even if you’re not vegetarian. There’s so much to like about it: the crispness of the eggplant, the crunch of the iceberg, the acid of the pickles, the velvety texture of the mayo with its tangy stack of herbs. And then there’s the deep, deep umami of the “magic sprinkle”. Still, for us, the shokupan is the real star here. It’s baked in-house, meaning it’s ultra-consistent, and able to be sliced thinly while maintaining its integrity. The eggplant sandwich was perhaps never going to outshine the schnitty – few sandwiches around town could, to be fair – but you still need to try it. And if you’re with a mate, the power move is of course to order both and split them between you. Where to get it The eggplant sandwich is $18.80. You can get one from 1007 Stanley Street East, East Brisbane; 173A Latrobe Terrace, Paddington; and Shop 203/142 Newmarket Road, Windsor.

David Jones’ private equity owners are on the cusp of appointing voluntary administrators as soon as Thursday morning after talks with major landlord Scentre fell over when the department store failed to pay rent for October. Westfield owner Scentre Group, which operates 17 shopping centres in which the prestige department store is located, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors, according to a source close to negotiations but not authorised to speak publicly. A deal to save the 188-year-old retailer David Jones may be unwinding. Louise Kennerley David Jones’ board directors are now assessing how long the 188-year-old retailer can continue trading before it appoints a voluntary administrator, which is expected to be McGrathNicol, the source said. Chief executive Erica Berchtold and board directors Phillip Cave and Simon Woodhouse, who are executive chair and managing partner at private equity firm Anchorage Capital respectively, were convening a board meeting on Wednesday evening, with a decision on voluntary administration expected to be made by Thursday morning.

Advertisement

Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since October and “therefore are in breach”. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it “We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading,” Rusanow said in a statement. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them.” David Jones’ initial restructuring deal to Scentre Group initially proposed handing over nine stores from February, keeping three stores at rents of 8 per cent of sales, continuing five stores on current terms, and unlocking $45 million in bank guarantees in exchange for equity. “It’s a straight financial calculation as to how they can continue trading,” the source said. “Do they meet the solvency test? They need to sit down and discuss the finances.”

Advertisement

David Jones’ failure to pay rent for October was a key flashpoint in why talks with Scentre Group fell over, a source said. Other commercial property landlords are also owed rent. A spokesman for David Jones confirmed that talks between the group and Scentre failed to resolve the impasse and talks had now concluded. “We know what you know.” A David Jones staff member who declined to be identified. The retailer’s stores in Westfield Parramatta, Warringah Mall, Carindale in NSW, Indooroopilly Shopping Centre, Robina Town Centre, Sunshine Plaza in Queensland, Westfield Marion in South Australia, Westfield Doncaster, Southland, Carousel, Booragoon in Victoria, and Karrinyup Shopping Centre in Western Australia are suspected as earmarked for closure, according to analysis by financial services firm MST Marquee.

A sense of impending trouble has already pervaded some stores. Loss-making store Westfield Parramatta in western Sydney was exceptionally quiet when this publication visited on Wednesday morning. Few shoppers were browsing across both levels of the store. The further in, the quieter it became.

Advertisement

At the back on level one, near the birthday cards and beds, temporary cardboard panels created a wall with a sign reading “staff only beyond this point”. Through gaps in the makeshift screen, shelves, mannequins and a selection of stock including Christmas trees and suitcases could be seen, stored away from the public eye. A makeshift wall set up in David Jones’ Parramatta store. Behind it is stock, shelves and mannequins. Signs advertising Black Friday sale offers, which expire in early December, had been collected and placed onto one of the counters. It’s unclear if staff were about to put them up or had just taken them down. Store staff were reluctant to talk and declined to confirm if it would be closing, with one employee saying: “We know what you know”. On Wednesday, David Jones’ lender Hilco said in a statement: “Hilco Capital has had no formal update on the status of negotiations.”

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘Alarming’: David Jones workers brace for job losses as store closures loom Hilco Capital confirmed last week that it had provided additional funding to see it through December, traditionally the most crucial time of the year for department stores. “Hilco Capital has funded above the agreed facility to allow David Jones to increase stock holdings ahead of the busy Christmas trade and sales period,” a Hilco spokesperson said. The group had also been negotiating with multiple landlords to slash its rent bill and close some loss-making stores. Lease and rent costs totalled $125 million for the 2025 financial year, but its debt burden also weighed heavily on the group with finance costs totalling $153 million, financial accounts released earlier this year show. Suppliers have told this publication they were already restricting the financial terms of sales to David Jones due to lengthening payment terms. They will become unsecured creditors and potentially lose significantly on any outstanding bills if the retailer goes into administration.

Advertisement

ASX-listed retailer Accent Group confirmed it moved to cash-on-delivery after outstanding unpaid invoices earlier this year, which David Jones has since resolved. Menswear label M.J. Bale ceased supplying David Jones’ online store, but still operates about nine concessions on the retailer’s premises. Dozens of premium and designer labels have jumped ship to rival Myer over the past few months. If David Jones collapses, Myer’s sales could be boosted by as much as $180 million and specialty retailers like JB Hi-Fi and Rebel may benefit from rent cuts, analysis from MST Marquee suggests. David Jones is the country’s 12th-largest retailer by floor space, ahead of Chemist Warehouse. “Myer has 12 stores within close proximity to the likely closed David Jones stores. Up to half of the lost David Jones sales could switch to Myer,” MST Marquee analysts said. “If landlords aren’t able to backfill the space effectively, lower rents across specialty retailers may result.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. A shark behaviour expert says a $100,000 Gold Coast plan for night surfing by floodlights near the mouth of a river known for bull sharks might not be such a great idea. Gold Coast City Council discussed trialling the concept – where three 24-metre-high lights would illuminate the water, so surfers can keep catching waves into the night – during next year’s World Surfing event at Snapper Rocks. The trial is part of a wider “Surfing Infrastructure Masterplan” hatched to maximise profit off the coast’s famous beaches, with the council keen to see how night surfing would work in action. Griffith University shark expert Vincent Raoult said bull sharks, which are known to be around the Tweed River outflow next to Snapper Rocks, are active at night, particularly between 4pm and 10pm.

Advertisement

Raoult said a one-off event would probably be fine, but more permanent or reoccurring night surfing at Snapper Rocks would be asking for trouble. “Anyone who has done any fishing knows that if you have lights on the side of the boat into the water, you’re going to bring up a whole host of bait fish, and often with those bait fish, you’ll have sharks coming in as well,” he said. Kelly Slater surfing at night … in the safety of his wave pool. Kenny Morris/World Surf League “Those floodlights will have essentially the same effect.” He said any plans should not be compared with France, where the WSL has held night surfing before.

“The key difference is in France there are no sharks,” he said. Related Article Triathlon Swim leg of Noosa triathlon cancelled after multiple shark sightings The plan was discussed in a transport and infrastructure meeting at the council on Tuesday, and follows the swim leg of the popular Noosa Triathlon being called off over the weekend due to shark sightings. Speaking with Nine News on Tuesday, councillor Gail O’Neill said precautions would be taken to make sure night surfing was safe. “With all the surfing events and all the surf life-saving events we have, people are on jet skis making sure sharks aren’t in the area,” she said.

But Raoult said the most successful shark-spotting tactic on the Gold Coast would be unavailable after dusk. “Drones can’t really work at night – you can’t really see through the water, and there are also some flight restrictions around operating drones at night,” he said. Jagadish Krishnan is having a bet both ways when he says he has done “everything appropriately” when declaring gifts, while simultaneously claiming he’s no longer a businessman outside parliament. An investigation by 9News and WAtoday revealed the WA Labor MP is being sued for $1 million in a US court. Riverton MLA Jagadish Krishnan. Hamish Hastie Wall Street investor Kannan Amalraj lent Krishnan the money for his wife’s businesses Spectrum Health and Codd Technology, and is now suing him, claiming he hasn’t paid it back. The American businessman also claims to have bankrolled Krishnan’s lavish trip to New York City in May 2024, covering thousands of dollars worth of expenses.

Advertisement

Accommodation, including a luxury $1000-a-night hotel metres from Times Square, limousine and taxi services, and a dinner cruise on the Hudson River. This masthead has seen receipts that back up some of these claims. The rest are detailed in a writ filed in the New Jersey District Court. All up, it totals approximately $6000 worth of alleged gifts. Nickels and dimes compared to the size of the loan, but what is in question is whether Krishnan should have declared it on the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. In a bizarre and hastily organised press conference last week, Krishnan defended himself, declaring he had “done everything appropriately in my declarations”. Under the Members of Parliament Act 1992, a member “shall disclose gifts received”, if they are valued at $500 or more. This includes travel undertaken by the member unless it “was made in the ordinary course of any trade, profession or vocation of the Member”.

Advertisement

He is claiming the travel gifts were for business purposes and exempt from declaration. But he has publicly declared he ceded his business roles when he entered parliament in 2021. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament Labor’s Riverton MP spends nearly entire salary on electorate expenses “Once I entered politics, I resigned from being a director,” Krishnan told 9News just last year, days out from the state election. “I have been out of business for almost four years.” He remains a shareholder of various interests, but the Australian Tax Office does not deem a shareholder to be a trade, profession or vocation.

Advertisement

Either, Krishnan is actually still involved in his businesses, which would absolve him of his responsibility to declare financial contributions. Or, he really is no longer a businessman, in which case he must declare the gifts. The Labor MP has snookered himself. Geoffrey Watson SC, director of Centre for Public Integrity, said MPs should regard their parliamentary role as their full-time employment. “They’re effectively an employee of the people of Western Australia,” he told WAtoday.

Advertisement

Or, in other words, a court case on the other side of the world does not absolve Krishnan of his responsibility and obligation to be accountable and transparent to his constituents. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament The US trip at the heart of WA Labor MP’s court fight over $1 million loan Krishnan has not responded to detailed questions about his financial dealings. Some are, understandably, covered by the fact that there are legal proceedings under way. But other unanswered questions are not, including is he bankrupt? (Which would render a member ineligible to sit in parliament). Let’s not forget that Krishnan was parliamentary secretary to the premier at the time of the trip – Roger Cook’s right-hand man – when he lobbied overseas investors for a big loan by any measure for his wife’s company, enjoying lavish gifts from an investor looking to sink his claws into the Australian market.

Advertisement

This masthead does not suggest he was on official parliamentary businesses while in the US, or that taxpayers footed any travel bill. Cook’s response when asked if Krishnan – and all members of his party – would face punishment if he hadn’t upheld the necessary standards of disclosures was unimpressively unconvincing. “That’s a hypothetical … that’s a decision for the caucus,” Cook said. The premier, like his colleagues, is watching this play out, because they aren’t sure which side of the court battle is telling the truth. For now, the US Federal Court will decide that.

Advertisement

But it does not say much if Cook cannot even tell his caucus to uphold basic parliamentary standards or face some sort of discipline. Let alone a parliamentary inquiry into Krishnan’s conduct.

Four years after Samoa was crushed in the World Cup final by Australia, captain Junior Paulo says he is desperate to avenge the loss and pull off the nation’s greatest win against the Kangaroos at Allianz Stadium on Sunday. “To lose a grand final like that … I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t burning for the guys who were there,” Paulo said of that 30-10 defeat at Old Trafford in 2022. The Kangaroos beat Samoa in the 2022 Rugby League World Cup final in England. Getty There’s been a few changes to the Samoan team in that time. Josh Papali’i has retired and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has gone from playing fullback to switching codes and joining the Wallabies. But the bulk of Samoa’s backline remains, including five-eighth and co-captain Jarome Luai, winger Brian To’o and centre Stephen Crichton. As does Spencer Leniu, who will again be injected off the bench to provide some spark and power.

Paulo, the 32-year-old 123kg wrecking-ball, said victory over Kevin Walters’ Kangaroos would rank among the country’s greatest feats. “It’s a privilege to be in this position for us,” he said. “It’s an opportunity to be a part of history and hopefully what can be one of the biggest upsets.” Junior Paulo says he has a “burning” desire to avenge the 2022 World Cup final defeat. Getty Images Paulo said fatigued would not be an issue, despite Samoa’s gruelling 20-18 defeat to Tonga being played 24 hours after the Kangaroos proved far too good for Karmichael Hunt’s Cook Islands. “We’ve had a good couple of days just to emotionally regulate [after the] immense pressure that came with the game as well,” Paulo said.

Advertisement

One area where Samoa will likely attack the Kangaroos is through the middle. New Zealand smashed Australia up front in their narrow 24-22 loss in the tournament opener, while Fiji and the Cook Islands also physically put Walters’ side under huge pressure. Former Kangaroos playmaker Luke Keary described Australia’s struggles in the middle as “concerning”. But Paulo downplayed the Kangaroos’ Achilles heel. “There’s still a quality forward pack right across the park,” he said.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, Australia centre Kotoni Staggs claims his decision not to sing the national anthem comes from a place of respect. Staggs and several fellow Australia team members have been criticised throughout the tournament because of their refusal to sing the pre-game anthem. Kotoni Staggs celebrates a try against the Cook Islands. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images The Brisbane centre received the backing of Broncos teammate Patrick Carrigan for his stance. Staggs, who has won nine caps for Australia since his debut in 2023, said: “I’m a proud Wirajudri boy and I’m proud of who I am and where I come from and me not singing an anthem doesn’t mean that I’m not grateful.

Advertisement

“I still love wearing that jersey, when the anthem is getting played you look around and get emotional. Kotoni Staggs celebrates his try. Getty Images “But me not singing, it’s a whole different meaning to that and that’s just me.” Staggs said his position on singing Advance Australia Fair came from a position of wanting to honour his ancestors. “Obviously in the past and what happened back in the day I’ve just learned from that,” Staggs said.

“You also talk to your elders from back home and grandparents and stuff like and [understand] what they had to go through, it’s more of a respect for my elders and my family. “I’m a proud Australian as well but at the end of the day it’s just something that I’ve lived by, and I’ve got no harm in it. It doesn’t take anything away from the jersey I wear.” Criticism of Staggs and other Indigenous Kangaroos stars, including Latrell Mitchell, is nothing new. Former Australian Test coach Mal Meninga previously defended players for their firm stance on the matter. Carrigan said athletes should have the right to stand up for what they believe in.

“As sports people there’s a focus on us as role models but it probably points to a greater conversation for us to have as a society outside of football,” Carrigan said. title: ‘Sad and devastated’: Canva cuts hit staff and Australian tech overall
text:

Analysis TechnologySoftware ‘Sad and devastated’: Canva cuts hit staff and Australian tech overall David Swan November 4, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Dunja Popovs woke up on Wednesday to the news that she was one of the 22 per cent of design software maker Canva’s workers losing their job. “Truthfully, I am sad and devastated, but I’m also extremely grateful that I ever had the opportunity in the first place,” Popovs, who led a team of content designers at Canva, wrote on LinkedIn. Her plan for now is “a whole lot of gardening”, then to start hunting for a new job. Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams at the Canva Create conference in Los Angeles in April. Canva chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Wednesday that 1271 people would be affected by a restructuring, aimed at resetting the business after growth started to slow this year.

Advertisement

Some will lose their jobs. Others will be asked to relocate or will find their roles rewritten. The timing was brutal: the news arrived a day after the Reserve Bank lifted rates to an 18-year-high. Anyone who has tried to get hired in tech knows not much happens between now and Australia Day. The news took me back to April, when I saw Canva close its biggest product launch ever in a Los Angeles football stadium with engineers in gold plastic crowns playing Ode to Joy on instruments that included a rubber duck. I asked co-founder Cliff Obrecht the question every Australian tech boss was getting that month. Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra were cutting thousands of jobs, much of it put down to AI. Was Canva next? The answer was definitive. “We do not have to do layoffs, and we don’t have any plans to do layoffs,” Obrecht said. Canva’s headcount growth had slowed from 50 per cent a year to under 5 per cent, and he pitched that as the grown-up alternative to what everyone else was doing. “Rather than this gas-on, hit-reverse, lay-off kind of mentality,” he said, “we’ve seen this coming, and we’ve just eased our foot off the accelerator.”

Advertisement

I believed him, and so did plenty of the people who got the email on Wednesday. One departing engineer described it as the “grim reaper of the tech world” arriving “a lot sooner than I thought it ever would”. Most staff were surprised, he said. To be fair to Obrecht, I think he meant every word. Canva had been profitable for nine straight years and had more than $US1.5 billion ($2.2 billion) in the bank. It had never needed to do major layoffs. Then the numbers turned, in large part due to the rapid rise of AI. In August, I reported that Canva had slowed that product launch because AI bills were eating its margins. Canva co-founder Cliff Obrecht. Peter Rae “Historically, the cost to create a design cost us essentially nothing,” Obrecht said in August. “The cost of goods to serve a user has gone from cents per month to many, many more cents.”

Advertisement

Canva’s internal valuation of its business, used to price staff shares, tumbled as a result, and Perkins’ email confirmed growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. She didn’t link the cuts directly to AI, but others are less sure the threat is temporary. Adam Barty, who runs Melbourne AI agency Revium, says it’s “pretty hard not to view AI as an existential threat to Canva’s core business model”, which is to give people who aren’t designers an easy way to make things free and convert enough of them into paying subscribers. Some long-term users have moved their slideshows and social posts to AI chatbots and barely open Canva anymore. For a decade, Canva has been the most successful story in Australian tech: a 19-year-old in Perth and her boyfriend, more than 100 investor rejections, then the most valuable start-up this country has produced. Its co-founders are now billionaires and every pitch deck in Surry Hills borrowed a little of its shine. Canva’s Cliff Orbrecht (left), Cameron Adams and Melanie Perkins. Getty

Advertisement

This setback is grim news for staff, but also for Australia’s venture capital sector, which has effectively been propped up by Canva’s outsized success. Related Article Updated

Software Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history Venture capital firm Blackbird owns about 10 per cent of Canva, and it has been a huge success for the firm until now. Airtree first invested in 2014 and has asked its own investors to keep its fund open until 2028 in the hope of a payday. Behind both firms sit wealthy families, endowments and super funds. If Canva’s value keeps sliding, so does the case that backing Australian start-ups is a sound use of retirement savings. Where things go from here is an open question, as is Canva’s very survival over the long term. An IPO looks further off than ever. A sale to a global tech giant near Canva’s current value could be an option and would be one of the biggest software deals ever done.

Advertisement

But there’s always a silver lining. When Google shut its Wave project (an attempt to build a social media platform for users to collaborate) in Sydney in 2010, a crop of talented engineers went looking for something new. One of them was Cameron Adams, who became Canva’s third co-founder. Canva is about to release a much bigger crop, with $US10,000 grants for anyone who wants to start their own business. If even a handful of those are successful, then Australian tech’s next big story started on Wednesday. David Swan travelled to Los Angeles in April with the support of Canva. title: Socceroos set Christmas deadline for Popovic decision as rival coaches circle
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerAsian Cup Socceroos set Christmas deadline for Popovic decision as rival coaches circle Vince Rugari November 4, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
