Football Australia is eager to have Tony Popovic’s future as Socceroos coach resolved before Christmas, but football boss Heather Garriock has warned that other candidates are “knocking at the door” as negotiations continue over a contract extension. Garriock, FA’s executive director of football and deputy CEO, told this masthead discussions were already under way with Popovic’s agent, Frank Trimboli, after the postponement of January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia threw the federation’s coaching plans into disarray. Loading Popovic turned down a four-year extension on the eve of the World Cup in favour of a short-term deal – partly because, as Garriock revealed last month on the Suited & Booted podcast, they could not reach agreement over financial terms. Garriock confirmed Popovic’s current contract actually expires in March, and does not automatically extend because the Asian Cup has been postponed by nearly 12 months. The tournament will now kick off on December 23, 2027 and run through to January 21, 2028, subject to FIFA approval.

Advertisement

FA’s immediate preference, Garriock said, is to retain Popovic at least until the end of the rescheduled Asian Cup – even if that means he could be in the dugout in September, when Australia’s qualification campaign for the 2030 FIFA World Cup begins, without any guarantee he would see it through. “We’ve already been speaking, even before this. That’s ongoing at the moment,” Garriock told this masthead. Socceroos coach Tony Popovic. Dominic Lorrimer “We need to do what’s best for both Football Australia and Tony, and they’re the discussions that we’re having at the moment. Our first priority is making sure that we both are happy with an extension for the Asian Cup. “We’ve got people knocking on our door, but we need to give Tony the best opportunity, because he’s actually delivered and done the business for Football Australia, he’s prepared the players amazingly well, and for us to give him the best opportunity to win a trophy for the Socceroos … it’s only fair.”

Advertisement

Garriock praised Popovic for the way he has strengthened the Socceroos’ brand, bolstered the national team’s player depth and re-established “accountability” for the Australian jersey. She also said his tenure – with Popovic having replaced Graham Arnold at short notice two years ago, at a precarious juncture in World Cup qualifying – showed changing coaches mid-cycle was not an impediment to success. Football Australia executive director of football and deputy CEO, Heather Garriock. Getty Images for Football Australia “Tony’s demonstrated that it’s not an absolute must,” she said. Popovic’s four-year contract offer from FA was not publicly known until he revealed it unprompted in a press conference in September – but he did not mention remuneration being a factor behind his decision to knock it back, simply saying a short-term renewal gave both parties flexibility to consider their positions after the Asian Cup.

Advertisement

Popovic also made clear at the time that he would be comfortable walking away from the national team after the Asian Cup, irrespective of the team’s performance, and that his own job security was not important to him. “I know the legacy that I’ll leave behind,” he said. “And if it’s someone else that takes it forward, that’s fine.” Asked about her comments on the podcast that “it came down to money”, Garriock said FA were restricted in what they could offer any national team coach. “We’re the governing body, and we need to live within our means,” she said. “We need to future-proof and make sure our business is sustainable. Unfortunately, we can’t pay what a club pays … it’s a vastly different role and an expectation to being paid at club level.”

Advertisement

The challenge with a 12-month extension for Popovic is that FA could miss out on other coaches who will become available in the coming months – in particular, Kevin Muscat, who is coming out of contract with Chinese club Shanghai Port at the end of the year and would be receptive to discussions over the Socceroos job if Popovic did not continue, sources said. “I think we need to get this put away by Christmas,” Garriock said. Other nations face similar dilemmas. Graham Arnold’s short-term contract with Iraq was also due to expire after the Asian Cup, while Japan had already announced that Hajime Moriyasu would hand over to Go Oiwa after the tournament. Both federations, like Australia, must now revisit their plans. Meanwhile, Popovic is set to unveil his squad on Friday for this month’s friendlies in the Middle East against Qatar and Jordan, which were to be their final warm-up games before the Asian Cup, and could yet be his final matches in charge of the Socceroos. Despite the uncertainty over the coaching position, Garriock said those would still be important fixtures to prepare the team for what lies ahead, including the new World Cup qualifying campaign.

Advertisement

Related Article Asian Cup Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos facing massive Popovic dilemma Some players, however, have expressed discomfort about the prospect of travelling to the region, according to sources close to the team, due to the deteriorating security situation. Garriock said any player would be excused from this window without any future repercussions if they chose not to go for those reasons. “It’s normal for both staff and players to be hesitant to want to travel to the Middle East at the moment,” she said. “However, we’ve got the best intelligence on the ground, and we wouldn’t put the players or staff at risk. It’s a matter for the players to decide whether they want to travel, and we’ll support their decision, both the players and staff – and it certainly won’t have an impact on selection going forward.”

NSW Origin forward Hudson Young has arrived in Port Moresby as the Chiefs continue their aggressive recruitment drive, desperate to lock up the injured Raider as their signing #008. Young, who is recovering from a season-ending Achilles injury, arrived on Wednesday in Port Moresby, where he was greeted by Chiefs coach Willie Peters, chief executive Lorna McPherson and general manager of football Michael Chammas. Canberra back-rower Hudson Young arrives in PNG. X Young made the trip with his manager Sam Ayoub in a clear sign they are ready to do business. It’s a tour that almost didn’t go ahead after the NRL initially set Young’s market value at $1.1 million, to match the amount Canberra was prepared to pay him. That figure was reset to $1 million before being re-evaluated again after the Raiders pulled the deal.

Advertisement

The Chiefs were never going to budge from their $900,000 per season offer, an amount which is now palatable to head office and Young himself given there are not any higher offers on the table. That was as high as the Chiefs were prepared to go after factoring in Young’s age (28), the serious Achilles injury he is recovering from and the other back-row options on the open market. Star Raiders forward Hudson Young, with PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters. PNG Chiefs Young is no stranger to PNG, having toured previously with the Prime Minister’s XIII side. However, this trip will be an opportunity to look at the working and living arrangements for Chiefs players before deciding whether the lifestyle suits him. While Young remains under contract to Canberra until the end of next season, relations between the parties have soured. The Raiders felt they had no option but to pull their offer – the highest the club has ever tabled to a player – after he continued to vacillate even after a fifth season was proposed.

Canberra coach Ricky Stuart, when asked if the Green Machine was prepared to release Young immediately, told The Canberra Times: “That’s up to Hudson and his management to ask for that, but I’d definitely look at it.” Whether another club could accommodate Young for a bridging year, before the Chiefs’ inaugural season in 2028, is unclear. Young said in September that the only clubs he would consider playing for were Canberra or PNG, although the landscape has shifted significantly since then. In-demand Titans forward Cooper Bai. Getty Images “It’s one of those things, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Young said at the time about the prospect of joining the Chiefs. “I just want to make sure that I’m comfortable with the decision I make, and that’s the reason why I’m going over there, just to suss it all out …

“It’s one of those things, I just want to see it for myself first. There’s been a lot of media around it and certain players going over there and saying certain things, so I just want to go over there and make the decision myself on what I feel.” Related Article NRL 2026 ‘We want a marquee halfback’: Chiefs ready to splash tax-free cash Now that they have entered their first free-agency period, the Chiefs are focusing on landing a halfback and assembling a strong forward pack. The Storm thought they had their man when Bai was last off contract, only for the 19-year-old to backflip and stay at the Titans during the 10-day cooling-off period. If you still have a David Jones gift card, now might be a good time to cash it in before the retailer’s board meets this evening and turns your voucher into the equivalent of a losing Melbourne Cup ticket. The board meeting is expected to perform last rites on what is left of the failing 188-year-old department store operator and put the company into voluntary administration. David Jones has run out of options after landlords refused a rescue deal for the department store operator. Ruby Alexander David Jones has run out of options and will need the protection of corporate undertakers to keep landlords and lenders at bay. But it won’t last long. Its major lender, Hilco Capital, will then appoint its own receiver to restructure and sell the business, and try to recoup its money.

Advertisement

That will involve drastic surgery to reduce the storied department store chain to a more modest store footprint – with lower rents – so that it just might remain viable. No one needs reminding how tough a job this will be. And not just based on the Reserve Bank’s latest interest rate rise this week. When the retailer’s payment troubles extended to its landlords last month, the writing was on the wall. Department stores globally have been under major pressure from online shopping, smaller and more nimble physical rivals and diminishing foot traffic as more people work from home. The headwinds have led to financial troubles, closures and bankruptcies across the globe, including at iconic Saks Fifth Avenue in New York. The worst cost-of-living crisis in decades may just be the final straw.

Advertisement

Research from MST Marquee published this week flagged a dozen store closures for David Jones, which would cost thousands of staff their jobs in the lead-up to Christmas. Related Article Updated

Retail On knife’s edge: David Jones could appoint administrators by Thursday The temptation would be to blame Anchorage Capital, the private equity firm that took the keys to the famous Australian department store more than three years ago. Who can forget the role Anchorage played in selling electronics group Dick Smith to the Australian public in 2013 at a massive profit, just a year after acquiring the business from Woolworths? Dick Smith collapsed in 2016. The fact that Anchorage paid just $100 million for David Jones in 2023 says plenty about how thin the veneer of viability was already by that stage.

Advertisement

Woolworths South Africa had spent $2.1 billion acquiring the struggling retailer in 2014, but its ownership was marred by quick CEO turnover and massive writedowns of a business clearly in decline. More significantly, Woolworths sold off David Jones’s property assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars to help ease the financial pain. This included the flagship Sydney and Melbourne stores. What Anchorage acquired for $100 million was a brand name, a turnaround plan and massive lease liabilities for stores that David Jones no longer owned. “The business is positioned as a premium and luxury offering with complementary services across fashion and beauty,” Anchorage said when it sealed the deal in 2023. David Jones was already implementing plans to spend $250 million on revamping its stores, its loyalty program, digital presence and customer relationship systems to boost sales and better compete with online retailers and luxury brands going direct to consumers.

Advertisement

That revamp was completed late last year, but it was not enough to turn the tide. Related Article Opinion

Retail How one David Jones supplier got paid when the others didn’t Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Suppliers have been ending exclusive deals with David Jones and defecting to rival Myer. And the group hit a cash crunch. By January, suppliers started complaining of delayed payment terms. In March, David Jones was late paying some suppliers and was pushing them all towards 60-day payment terms. In effect, it was using suppliers as a de facto bank, using proceeds from the sale of their goods for extended amounts of time before paying its bills.

Advertisement

“We note that recent media commentary is best characterised as misinformed – like many businesses, David Jones is adjusting some operational processes to best position the business for sustainable, long-term growth,” a spokesperson for Anchorage said at the time. When the retailer’s payment troubles extended to its landlords last month, the writing was on the wall for its continued survival. There was no way a shrewd operator like Westfield-owner Scentre was going to agree to hand over tens of millions of dollars worth of bank guarantees – designed to protect it from rent default – for shares in the failing department store operator. These shares will be worthless when Anchorage calls in the administrators. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

title: In Beijing, Mbappé’s face still spruiks drinks amid broadcast blackout

Beijing: On the streets of Beijing, the French footballer Kylian Mbappé’s face still peeks out from the chilled drinks cabinets of China Post-owned newsstands. From behind the glass fridge doors, a smiling Mbappé graces bottles of peach-flavoured sport drinks that promise to quench thirst and replenish electrolytes. They are clearly visible to passers-by, with front-row billing alongside bottles of green tea, energy drinks and Coca-Cola. A kiosk in Beijing’s Chaoyang district sells the Mbappé-promoted sports drink after the Real Madrid star was forced to apologise for remarks about a meme comparing him to Mao Zedong. Lisa Visentin But Mbappé’s face was absent from Chinese televisions this past weekend. Fans who wanted to see him slot an 11th-minute penalty against Racing Santander in the Spanish LaLiga match on Sunday were denied the chance. China’s state broadcaster CCTV did not air the match, despite a broadcast deal with LaLiga, Spain’s professional soccer league, amid an ongoing fallout over the Real Madrid star’s perceived slight against China’s founding leader Mao Zedong. The great cancellation has not yet trickled down to street vendors.

Advertisement

A short walk through the inner suburbs of Beijing’s Chaoyang district revealed at least three kiosks and one supermarket were stocking the Mbappé-endorsed drink this week, after beverage giant Dongpeng joined several other Chinese companies in severing promotional deals with the star. “I only saw the news about this in passing, so I don’t know exactly what he [Mbappé] said,” said 56-year-old Shi, who manages one China Post-owned street kiosk. She had restocked her drinks cabinet with more Mbappé drinks since the weekend but was not sure whether the supplier would send more once this stock was sold. Kylian Mbappe upset some Chinese people by laughing at a meme depicting him as Mao Zedong. Jamie Brown However, her views on Mao help explain the genesis of the outrage, even as many Chinese people remain in the dark about the details of Mbappé’s remarks, which have been blocked by government censors, deemed too egregious to be broadcast to the masses.

Advertisement

“As a Chinese person, I grew up listening to Chairman Mao’s songs and quotations. My love and affection for Chairman Mao are beyond question,” Shi said. ‘My feelings for Chairman Mao are not something I can express in words; it’s something ingrained in my bones.’ Shi, Beijing kiosk manager “I’m almost 60 now. It may be different for younger generation today. My feelings for Chairman Mao are not something I can express in words; it’s something ingrained in my bones.” At another kiosk a few hundreds metres away, the operators also had no knowledge of the Mbappé scandal and no one had advised them to stop selling the Mbappé-promoted drinks, they said. “We don’t know about it,” said the kiosk manager, who declined to give his name, while his colleague pulled out her phone to search the news. “These are matters of state. I’m not interested in that. All I care about is whether I can make any money at my shop today. National affairs are for the state to handle. They don’t have much to do with ordinary people like us.”

Advertisement

A 1960s poster of Mao Zedong. Getty Images The Real Madrid striker was forced to issue an apology last week for a months-old interview in which he laughed at a meme depicting him as “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. Real Madrid and LaLiga president Javier Tebas also issued apologies. Related Article Inside China ‘Not accepted. Not forgiven!!’ : French superstar’s ‘dictator Mao’ meme ignites fury in China The meme in question showed Mbappé’s face photoshopped onto Mao’s body — one of many viral memes that depict the footballer as different dictators from history, in a joke that taps into his commanding presence inside teams. Mao, who led China from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains widely revered by many in China. He is credited for ending China’s domination by imperialist forces and heralding its independence.

Advertisement

Discussion of his legacy is tightly controlled by Chinese authorities, especially when it comes to the catastrophic impact of the industrialisation campaign known as the Great Leap Forward in the late 1950s and early ’60s, and the ensuing famine that killed millions of people, and the Cultural Revolution from 1966 which triggered widespread violence and bloodshed. The scandal has exposed the paradox of the Chinese censorship system that fanned the flames of outrage while blocking the original content that would allow citizens to reach their own verdict, triggering some to go looking for answers. ‘What exactly did Mbappe do? I can’t find anything about it.’ Weibo post To access the video of Mbappé’s interview, Chinese citizens need to use a virtual private network (VPN) to jump the Great Firewall that blocks them from accessing the Western internet, an act that is technically prohibited in China. Kylian Mbappe celebrates after scoring his side’s opening goal during a Spanish La Liga soccer match in Spain, Sunday on October 25, 2026. AP

Advertisement

On social media, some people demanded that vendors cover up Mbappé’s face on the drinks packaging; others were perplexed about the origins of the scandal. “What exactly did Mbappe do? I can’t find anything about it,” one person posted on Chinese microblogging site Weibo. “Just search for it on the internet beyond China’s firewall and you’ll find it. They don’t let you see it on the Chinese internet...,” another user responded. It remains unclear when the broadcast blackout will end and Real Madrid games will be aired again in China. Government-owned China Media Group (CMG) said last week that “Mbappé’s outrageous remarks have harmed the Chinese people, crossed a line and exceeded the scope of freedom of speech”.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
